Before Herman Sachtjen, Reserve Circuit Judge
- - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -
Two actions to review decisions of the Industrial Commission by the
above named plaintiffs were brought on for hearing and determination by the
Court, The action in which John E. Bandar, et al, are plaintiffs relates to
a decision of the Industrial Commission, dated February 22, 1963, which
affirmed the findings and decision of an Appeal Tribunal under date of
December 12, 1962.
The action in which Clarence W. Shebesta is plaintiff relates to a
decision of the Industrial Commission, dated June 7, 1963, which affirmed
the findings of an II ppeal Tribunal dated May 15, 1963. •
The action in which John E. Bandar, et al, are plaintiffs is the
important one and if the Court sustains the Findings and Decision of the
Commission therein, it will also be controlling in the Shebesta case. It also,
by stipulation, is agreed that it is a 11pilot II case and will govern the
rights of about 300 other employees similarly situated.
This litigation grows out of the fact that on April 28, 1962, the
defendant, Sw-i_ft & Company, closed its plant in Milwaukee, terminating about
600 employees. At the time of closing, the defendant company paid such
employees certain sums of money, which represented the following:
(a) Earned but unpaid vacation pay; (b) Sepe.ration allowance; and
(c) Gratuity pay.

Four of the above named plaintiffs, Bandar, Cabbell, Nicholson and
Switzer, were employees, who were entitled to vacation pay and separation
allowance; two, Maren and Weisman, were employees entitled to vacation pay
and gratuity pay; and one, Roman J. Listwan, was only entitled to separation
allowance.
In the other action where Clarence W. Shebesta is plaintiff, he was an
employee who was entitled to both a vacation and separation allowance.
No question is raised as to the correctness of the amount of moneys
paid by the defendant Swift & Company to them for these various benefits,
but the plaintiffs are aggrieved at the decisions and orders of the
Industrial Commission that deprived them of their right to receive
unemployment compensation benefits during various weeks which were subsequent
to the closing of defendant's plant in Week 17 of 1962.
The Industrial Commission's decision held that each of the plaintiff
employees received "wages" in the form of vacation pay, dismissal or
termination pay, subsequent to Week 17 of 1962; that for each week in which
"wages II were received, the plaintiff employees were ineligible for
unemployment benefits, pursuant to Secs. 108,05(4)(b) and 108.05(5) of the
Stats. of 1961, because the payments in the form of vacation pay, dismissal
or termination pay, were definitely allocated and payable to the plaintiff
employees by the close of the weeks for which such payments were made, and
that each plaintiff employee had due notice of such allocation at not less
than Lis approximate full weekly wage rate.
Plaintiffs contend that the Industrial Commission was in error in making
the above decision; that both the statutes referred to in the above decision
and the Master Agreement entered into by Swift & Company under date of
September 16, 1961, with their employer did not authorize the allocation
of these benefits as "wages" so as to deprive them of unemployment compensation
benefits in the weeks subsequent to the closing of the plant.
In the event that it be determined that the defendant Swift & Company
had the right to make the above allocation, it is further contended that it
did not give to the plaintiffs due and proper notice as required by Secs.
108.05(4)(b) and 108.05(5) so as to make the allocation effective.
The Appeal Tribunal made very full and complete findings on all the
issues presented with reasons supporting them. These findings were approved
and adopted by the Commission as its findings, most of which are based on
uncontradicted testimony and accordingly are supported by evidence.
The following are the basic ones which give rise to the present
controversy:
"The employer is engaged in the meat packing business and operated
a packing division in Milwaukee employing about 600 production workers.
"The employes were members of a union that represented them in
negotiations with the employer. Sometime in February, 1961 union representatives
received official notice from the employer that the Milwaukee packing division
would cease operations completely at some undetermined future date.
2

"Nearly a year thereafter, on January 23rd, 1962 (Week 4) the employer
addressed and mailed a letter to all production workers giving each of
them notice that the Milwaukee packing division would cease production
operations on Saturday, April 28, 1962 (Week 17) and that they would become
unemployed after that date,
"Pursuant to the terms of the employment contract entered into on
September 16, 1961, by and between the union and the employer, certain
remunerative benefits became vested in the employes at the time they became
unemployed, These benefits included vacation pay, separation allowance,
and a payment known as I gratuity pay' , 11
Plaintiffs do not challenge the correctness of the computation for the
above benefits and that they received them, all in accordance with the contract
of employment, They strenuously dispute the right of the defendant to
allocate the payments to weeks subsequent to the closing of the plant so as
to deprive them of unemployment compensation benefits for those weeks,
It appears to the court that these benefits fall into two different
categories, Vacation pay benefits are paid annually to employees and
contemplate the return of the employees to their former employment when
their vacation period is over, While separation pay and gratuity or
termination pay is given when there is a final severance of employment,
Vacation pay, by virtue of Sac. 108,05(4)(b) Stats,, for benefit
purposes is treated as "wages" provided it is properly allocated, l\.nd our
court has held that unless a collective bargaining agreement contains
limitations upon the employer's discretionary right at common law in setting
time for vacations, the employer has absolute discretion in establishing
the time for vacations even though the amount of pay and length of vacation
is prescribed by such agreement.
DarlinfLvs. Industrial Comm,, 4 Wis. (2d) 345, 361.
Qutler-Hammer, Inc. vs. Industrial Comm,, 13 Wis, (2d) 618.
Plaintiffs claim that the defendant Swift did not possess the power
under the Collective Bargaining Agreement to allocate the vacation pay to
the period immediately subsequent to the plant shut-down; and that in
accordance with their former practice under the agreement and its action and
conduct up to the time of the shut-down it should be stopped from exercising
that right.
The provision in respect to vacation pay under the agreement, as far
as material to the controversy, provided as follows:
''Vacatiomwill, as far as practical, be granted for the period
selected by the employs, but final allocation of vacation periods is left
to the company in order to assure orderly operation of the plant, 11
It is contended by the plaintiffs that the only power the defendant
Swift possessed under the foregoing provision to fix vacation time was that
necessary to assure the orderly operation of the plant, Once the plant
closed, vacation time thereafter would not affect the orderly operation
of the plant, and the right of the employes to select their vacation time
thereafter became absolute in them.
3

The commission found that:
"This provision was clearly intended to apply to a plant in operation
and since the plant was no longer in operation, such contract provision
must be deemed to be inapplicable and the employer retained its common
law right to allocate the vacation pay to periods after the plant shutdown, 11
This is a conclusion of law and undoubtedly the crucial one in respect to
the allocation of vacation pay, The court has previously stated that vacation
pay falls in a different category than separation or termination payments,
Vacation with pay is granted annually and contemplates the return of the
employee to his former employment, It is a respite from, so many times, an
arduous and monotonous employment and its aim is to build a healthy morale
and incentive to do better work for their employer.
The above provision as to vacation pay is the same as appeared in the
former collective bargaining agreement when there was no contemplation of
a plant closing, The court is of the opinion that the commission's
determination that this provision was applicable only to the plant while
in operation and not applicable when it ceased operation is reasonable,
The very purpose of paid vacations is defeated on a shutdown, The services
of the employees are completely and finally terminated, It is impossible
to be on vacation when the employer ia no longer in operation.
The plaintiffs further complain that the vacation pay provision was
inserted in the agreement after there was a contemplation of the plant
closing; that after the plant closing was announced and before the vacation
pay clause was agreed to, considerable negotiations were being held between
the Bargaining Committee of the Union representing the employees and
defendant Swift & Company on this very issue, It is, therefore, contended
that if the defendant wanted the absolute right to designate the vacation
periods, it could have contracted for that, or it could have modified the
right of the employees to select their own vacation times, It did neither
and now it should not be allowed to claim the right,
The commission made no specific finding in respect to this issue but
made general findings with respect to all negotiations had between union
representatives and management representatives from the time it was
announced of the plant closing to the time it shut down 13 months later
and concluded that the management made no commitment in respect to the
allocation of vacation pay and other benefits. The allocation of vacation
pay and other benefits was the paramount issue in the minds of the union
representatives in all these negotiations. They wanted them allocated
by the defendant so that their employees would not be deprived of immediate
unemployment compensation. The fact that it was not inserted in the clause
governing vacation pay, was clear proof that the defendant did not accede
to such demand and that it reserved the right to make the allocation it did,
A different issue may have been presented if the plaintiffs had chosen
their vacation weeks prior to the shutdown. It is claimed by the plaintiffs
that they were prevented or persuaded not to do so. It is pointed out that
in former years under the same vacation pay provisions as the one in the
contract dated September 16, 1961, the defendant SWift & Company immediately
after the first of each year, posted charts in the various departments,
whereupon the employees could choose their vacation weeks for the ensuing
year. This was not done in 1962, Also, two of the plaintiffs testified
4

that when they asked about choosing their vacation weeks, they were told by
their foreman not to take them until after the plant closing, because then
they would be able to get both vacation pay and unemployment compensation,
It is undisputed that none of the plaintiffs chose their vacation
weeks prior to the shutdown, The commission made no finding in respect
to the failure of the employer to post charts at the beginning of the
year 1962. The reason for not doing so is plain, There was no need for
it. The commission made the following finding, which is undisputed:
"On January 23, 1962 (Week 4) the employer addressed and mailed a
letter to all production workers giving each of them notice that the
Milwaukee packing division would cease production operations on Saturday,
April 28th (Week 17), and that they would become unemployed after that date, 11
Whether there was an oral agreement entered into between authorized
employer representatives and the union officials which prompted the foremen
to advise the two employees, as above stated, not to take their vacations
till after the shutdown, the commission answered as follows:
"It was further contended that the employer Is method of allocation
was contrary to an oral agreement entered into between authorized employer
representatives and union officials. Such contention was not established, 11
The court has examined the entire record on this issue and the only
testimony that could be found on establishing an oral agreement was the
testimony of two of the plaintiffs with their foremen as above stated,
Of course such conversation was net between authorized representatives of
the employer and union officials and therefore not binding.
The Appeal Tribunal made detailed findings of the various meetings had
between union and management officials where the paramount issue was the
allocation of benefits upon the plant's closing, It covered a 13 month
period, The union was unsuccessful in having their request inserted in
the Master Agreement of September 16, 1961, The union, however, continued
their endeavor-a to have the management representatives grant their request
but as the commission found, "management representatives made no commitment
to union representatives as to its intentions with respect to acceding to
such request. 11 In other words, it appears that while the management
representatives never said, 11No,11 still they never said, 11Yes. 11 No doubt
the purpose of this uncertainty was to instill in the minds of the employees
a hope that all would be well and thus produce better working conditions in
the plant before its closing, It may have been the same reason that
prompted the foremen to tell what the two plaintiffs testified was told them.
Of course, hope and wishful thinking does not create a legal enforceable
right, The union officials were not mislead. They informed members
attending two membership meetings dt!ring the last month that the plant was
in operation that the employer was going to allocate the payment of benefits
to the weeks of unemployment immediately following the plant shutdown.
For the foregoing reasons the findings and determination of the
Industrial Commission in respect to the allocation of vacation pay benefits
are affirmed.
5

The court will next consider plaintiffs_l grievances in respect to the
commission's findings and determination of separation and gratuity payments"
It is contended that the commission erred in finding and determining that
gratuity pay was dismissal or termination pay and that it also erred in
further finding and determining that that separation pay and gratuity pay
could be allocated as wages, so as to deprive them of unemployment
compensation benefits following the plant shutdown.
Plaintiffs contend that "gratuity pay" is something different than
other separation, termination or dismissal allowances. It was payable
to those employees who were between the ages of 55 and 65 who were eligible
for a company pension. They were paid in a lump sum based on a straight
eight weeks' wages. It is claimed that such was a bonus payment, a reward
for past services.
The commission, however, based its determination on the language
employed in the Master Agreement (Ex. 8, p. 154), It reasoned the
following:
"The contract provision in question does not itself use the term
'gratuity pay' but uses the term 'eight weeks pay' which is given to
those employes 'whose services are terminated by the company because of
the closing of a department or plant and who are entitled to receive a
pension under the Swift & Company Pension Trust. 111
And for that reason it deemed "gratuity pay" to be simply dismissal or
termination pay and therefore wages under .Sec. 108,05(5) of the statutes.
The court is of the opinion that this reason is sound. It was not paid
out of the pension fund. It is a larger remuneration than that given to
those employees who receive separation pay, but it is for the same purpose.
While there are no Wisconsin Supreme Court cases bearing on this issue,
the Commission cites in its brief a North Carolina Supreme Court case to
support its position. In that case the court said:
"Claimant Daniel McClain was paid for a four weeks I vacation and
given a gratuity of $688.80, equal to eight weeks' wages, which payments
sufficed to bring him in the class of employes entitled to retirement pay.
We think these payments to him fall in the ssme category as the payments
made to the other claimants." In.._:th§._mat-ter of Tvson, et al, and Swift
& Companz, 251 N.C. 662, 117 S.E. (2d) 854.
The further question then arises, and perhaps the most serious and
difficult one in this action, and that is the allocation of these payments.
The commission held that the defendant Swift & Company had the right to
allocate them so as to deprive the plaintiffs from unemployment compensation
benefits for the weeks covered by them immediately following the plant
shutdown.
It is contended by the plaintiffs that these payments were given for
past services rendered by them; that said payments were meant to compensate
them for the loss of seniority rights, pension rights, hospital, surgical,
medical and insurance rights, and other rights, credits and privileges set
forth in the bargaining contract which had accrued to them over the period
of time they were employed. They cite cases to support this position.
6

The issue has never been passed upon by our Supreme Court,
The commission considered that separation allowances, dismissal pay and
termination pay are synonymous terms; that separation allowances are not
payments for past services or that the employe has a vested right in them.
It points to the Master Agreement, Sec, 71, (Ex, 8) wherein there are
listed six circumstances under which such payments are not to be paid, If
an employee is discharged for misconduct or if he voluntarily resigns, he is
not entitled to separation pay under this agreement, If these payments were
for past services and the employee had a vested right in them, the termination
of employment or its cause would be immaterial and ineffective,
The court agrees with the re;isoning of the commission that 11The whole
idea and spirit of severance pay is with respect to the future, 11 It is a
sum of money, in addition to any accrued wages or salaries for past work, paid
to an individual whose employment is terminated through no fault of his own.
The most common objective of dismissal pay plans has been to ease such
employee's financial burden while he is looking for a new jab, or while he
may be training himself in new skills so as to enable him to secure employment.
The longer the worker has been on the job for the particular employer, the
further he will have himself removed from the general labor market; hence,
the longer it may take him to acquire new skills and find new employment.
Therefore, the amount of these payments are keyed accordingly, Sec, 7l(d)
of Exhibit 8, the Agreement, establishes that it was the intention of the
parties that these payments were to be on a weekly basis.
The court is of the opinion that under the statutory law of Wisconsin,
Secs, 108,02(6) and 108.05(5), and as interpreted by the court in vacation
pay cases in Qfil:ling vs. Industrial Comm. (supra) and .Qutler-Hammer Inc. vs,
Industrial Comm, (supra), the Commission did not commit any error in deciding
that the defendant Swift & Company had the authority under the Master
Agreement (Ex. 8) and the statutory law of this state to allocate the
separation and gratuity payments to weeks subsequent to the plant shutdown,
The defendant had not bargained away this right, There was much agitation
on the part of the union representatives prior to the signing of the Master
Agreement (Ex. 8) in respect to the allocation of vacation and separation
payments so that it would not interfere and prevent the immediate payment
of unemployment compensation benefits on the plant's shutdown. The
defendant did not accede to such request and no provision was inserted
in the Master Agreement, The plaintiffs then contend that defendant Swift
agreed to this contractual provision at a time when plans were already
made to close its plant, It is pointed out that the defendant Swift could
have conditioned the payments of separation allowances in such a way as to
permit the plaintiffs to receive the full payment thereof without losing
their unemployment compensation benefits, and its failure to do so should
be a bar and should have prevented it from making the allocation it did.
There was no duty on the part of the defendant to assert this right. The
law accorded him that right with or without a contract. Sec. 108,05(5) Stats.
It is true that an employer can relinquish this right by contract. This is
what the plaintiffs through the bargaining representatives of the union
sought to have done, both before the signing of the contract of employment,
Exhibit 8, and thereafter for a period of 12 months. But they did not succeed,
It is true that there are cases that appear to support plaintiffs'
position, that dismissal or separation payments do not disqualify an employee
7

from unemployment compensation benefits as cited in their brief. But those
cases are found in jurisdictions that do not have the statutory provisions
found in Wisconsin Secs. 108.02(6) and 108.05(5), and are not controlling.
The last assignment of error is that the defendant did not give the
proper notice as required by Sec. 108.05(5) to the class of employees
represented by the plaintiffs John J. Maren and Andrew Weisman, These
employees were entitled to a company pension, vacation pay and gratuity
pay, and were about 200 in number, It is admitted and the commission
found, "that no ~ritten notice of the allocation of payments to these
employes was given. 11
These employees were an older class of employees than the other
plaintiffs and were given individual interviews by one Walter Meyer,
former Industrial Relations Manager of the defendant Swift & Company. He
testified and the commission found that in these individual interviews, he
told each of the employees, "that the four week vacation payment and the
eight week gratuity payment would be allocated to the first twelve weeks
following his dismissal from work and that thereafter he could collect
unemployment compensation and pension benefits."
This finding is supported by credible evidence. Certainly John J. Maren
cannot complain about this finding. (See Ex. 18). The statute does not
require that a written notice be given, as the attorneys for the plaintiffs
contend, It does require that a due notice be given. The purpose of the
statute is to inform the employe who is to receive vacation and separation
benefits the amount of such wages and to what weeks they have been
allocated and payable, so that at the end thereof, if he remains unemployed,
he can collect unemployment compensation benefits, ,QY!l, means t imely, at
or before such payments are received. No claim was made by any of these
employees that they lost any right or suffered any wrong because of a lack
of notice.
For the foregoing reasons the court is satisfied that all the findings
of fact complained of in this action are supported by credible evidence
and th~t the construction and determination of legal principles involved
in the controversy by the commission are sound and reasonable.
In re Roman J. Listwan and Clarence W. Shebesta, the plaintiff in the
other action, it is conceded that while the factual situations in their
cases are at variance, the issues and principles are the same as the other
plaintiffs. Therefore, the findings and determination of the commission
in respect to these plaintiffs are likewise affirmed.
In the separate action wherein Clarence W. Shebesta is the plaintiff,
the reasons above stated may be incorporated by reference and controlling
in that action,
The Attorney General may prepare the proper judgments in both actions
in accordance with the above directions, and will submit the same to opposing
counsel before presenting it to this court for signature.
Dated: June 24, 1964.
HERMAN W, SACHTJEN
Reserve Circuit Judge

title: LIRC Unemployment Insurance Decision — Brauneis
text:
STATE OF WISCONSIN CIRCUIT COURT MILWAUKEE COUNTY
•··
BRANCH 32
TODD W. BRAUNEIS, et al.,
Petitioners,
'fl-'l9
V. Case No. 97-CV-00~
STATE OF WISCONSIN,
LABOR AND INDUSTRY REVIEW COMMISSION;
FILED
and THE ILLINGWORTH CORPORATION,
Respondents. 34 JUN 3 0 1998 34
JON W. SANFILIPPO
DECISION AND ORDER ActinQ Clerk of Circuit Court
BACKGROUND
The petitioners are employees of the Illingworth Corporation (Illingworth) who belong
to Local 18 of the Sheet Metal Workers International Association (Local 18) for the purposes
of collective bargaining. During negotiations, Illingworth is represented by a collective_
bargaining organization known as the Sheet Metal and Air Conditioning Contractors'
Association of Milwaukee (the Association).
Members of the Association assign exclusive rights to the Association to negotiate
contracts with Local 18. Members also agree to act as directed by the Association in the
event of a labor dispute, i.e. closing the doors to their facilities.
On June 6, 1996, the collective bargaining agreement between Local 18 and the
Association expired. The following day, Local 18 members employed at Construction
Supply and Erection Corporation (CS&E). also a member of the Association, commenced a
1

strike at CS&E's facilities. At no time were petitioners directly involved with the strike at
CS&E, nor did petitioners commence a strike at the Illingworth facility.
On June 11, 1996, the Association instructed its members, including Illingworth, to
bar their union employees from reporting to work.' The petitioners were not permitted to
return to work until the strike at CS&E ended on June 14, 1996.
Petitioners applied for unemployment compensation benefits for the period they were
not permitted to report to work. The Petitioners were granted benefits in the initial
determination. Illingworth appealed, but the Appeal Tribunal affirmed. Illingworth again
appealed and the State of Wisconsin ·Labor and Industry Review Commission (LIRC)
reversed the Appeal Tribunal. The petitioners now appeal LIRC's decision to deny them
unemployment compensation benefits arguing that they were "locked out" as defined by
section 108.04(100(b), Stats ..
STANDARD OF REVIEW
LIRC' s findings of fact will be upheld if they are supported by credible and
substantial evidence. Hagen v. LIRC, et al .. 210 Wis. 2d 12, 23, 563 N.W.2d 454 (1997).
In reviewing a LIRC decision regarding a question of law, there are three levels of deference
which may be applied: great weight, due weight, or de novo review. Hamischfeger Corp. v.
LIRC, 196 Wis. 2d 650, 660, 539 N.W.2d 98 (1995).
The great weight standard is applied when four requirements are met:
1To eliminate any confusion, the ten:n "lock out" will only be used in a manner consistent with section
108.04(10)(d), Stats.
2

1) The agency must be charged by the legislature with the duty of administering
the statute;
2) The interpretation of the agency must be one of long-standing;
3) The agency must have employed its expertise or specialized knowledge in
forming the interpretation; and
4) The agency's interpretation must provide uniformity and consistency in the
application of the statute.
The due weight standard is applied when the agency has some experience in the area,
but not enough to put it in a better position to interpret the statute than the court. UFE Inc.
and Pacific Indemnity Co. v. LIRC and Jerry Huebner, 201 Wis. 2d 274, 286, 548 N.W.2d
57 (1995). The court may overturn the agency's interpretation, even if it is reasonable, if
the court believes there is a better interpretation of the statute. Id. The court only applies the
de novo standard in situations where the issue before LIRC is clearly one of first impression,
or where the LIRC's position on the issue has been so inconsistent as to provide no guidance.
UFE at 285.
The issues before the court are certainly ones of first impression. The first issue
currently before the court involves an interpretation of section 108.04(10)(d), Stats.,
. regarding what is meant by "a union or group of employees of the employer". While LIRC
may have experience in interpreting much of section 108.04 Stats., the statutory provision
has not been extensively examined. To date, only one published case, Trinwith et al., v.
LIRC, 149 Wis. 2d 634, 439 N.W.2d 581(Ct. App. 1996), examined the language of section
108.04(10)(d), and even then, the court only addressed the issue of whether a failure to
3

extend a wage rate constituted a "lockout". 2
The second issue deals with whether a strike against one member of an employer
association constitutes a strike against all. LIRC has not demonstrated any lengthy
experience in addressing this issue. Therefore, because the issues before the court are one of
first impression, the court's review in this action is de novo.
ANALYSIS
I. According to Wisconsin Statutes, no strike occurred against the Association or
Illingworth.
LIRC presumed that a strike against one member of the Association was a strike
against all members of the Association and therefore, a strike against the Association itself.
However, because the Local 18 members employed at CS&E are only employes of CS&E
and not of the Association or Illingworth, it would be impossible for CS&E employes to
commence a strike against the Association .
The Association is a corporation, separate and distinct from its member companies. It
is an agent of the individual employers; it does not own the member companies. The
Association was formed for the sole purpose of representing the individual companies in
negotiations with Local 18. There is no evidence in the record to support a finding that the
@£)cites Piller et al v, LIRC et al., LC88-CV-8-591, an unpublished decision that was reversed on
appeal, to support its interpretation of section 108.04(10)(d) Stats. It should be noted that pursuant to section
809.23(3) Stats., unpublished Court of Appeals decisions may not be used as precedent, nor can it be used as
persuasive authority. Such use of unpublished decisions has been found to be sanctionable. See Beaupre v.
Aireiss, 208 Wis. 2d 238, 244 {Ct. App. 1997), Tamminen v. Aetna Cas. and Surety Co., 109 Wis. 2d 536,
563-564 (1982).
4

individual employers were ever agents of the Association. • Therefore, the employes of the
individual companies cannot be said to be employes of the Association.
Section 108.02 (12), Stats., defines "employe" as "any individual who is or has been
performing services for an employing unit, in an employment, whether or not the individual
is paid directly by such employing unit..." Section 108.02(15) defines "employment" as
"any service, including service in interstate commerce, performed by an individual for pay."
The employees of the individual companies are not employees of the Association.
They do not perform services for the Association nor are their wages paid by the
Association. Pursuant to section 108.02(15), Stats., the members of Local 18 are only
employees of the individual companies for whom they work. Consequently, the strike could
not have been against the Association.
Throughout the statutes, "strike" is defined as "any concerted stoppage of work by
employes, and any concerted slowdown or other concerted interruption of operations or
services by employes, or any concerted refusal of employes to work or perform their usual
duties as employes for the purpose of enforcing demands upon an employer."
Secs. 49.141(l)(L), 49.19(1), 111.15(1)(b),lll.70(1), &111.81, Stats. Because the CS&E
employees were not employees of the Association, they could not strike against the
Association. Thus, the concerted work stoppage was against CS&E only and done only by
CS&E employes.'
By this same token, the employees who went on strike against CS&E could not be
said to be employes of Illingworth. First, CS&E employes do not perform services for
3conversely, an act by the employer could not be considered at act against all union members,
regardless of whether they are employed by the employer.
5

Illingworth, either paid or unpaid. Second, given the definition of "strike" discussed above,
it would be impossible for CS&E' s employees to go on strike against Illingworth because,
they are not Illingworth's employes and could not promulgate a work stoppage at Illingworth.
Therefore, no strike took place against Illingworth.
II. Section 108.04(10)(d) is ambiguous.
Section 108.04 Stats. states in relevant part:
(a) An employe who has left or partially or totally lost his or her work
with an employing unit because of a strike or other bona fide labor
dispute, other than a lockout, is not eligible to receive benefits based on
wages paid for employment prior to commencement of the dispute for
any week in which the dispute is in active progress in the establishment
in which the employe is or was employed, except as provided in par.
(b).
(d) In this subsection, "lockout" means the barring of one or more
employes from their employment in an establishment by an employer as
a part of a labor dispute, which is not directly subsequent to a strike or
other job action of a labor union or group of employes of the employer,
or which continues or occurs after the termination of a strike or other
job action of a labor union or group of employes of the employer.
In other words, pursuant to Section 108.04(10)(d), the act of barring employees from
their employment constitutes a "lock out" when the act 1) is a part of a labor dispute, 2) is
NOT directly subsequent to a strike or other job action and 3) the strike or job action
precipitating the act was committed by a labor union or group of employees of the employer.
Ambiguity arises in the phrase, "subsequent to a strike or other job action of a labor
6

union or group of employes of the employer". The disjunctive could be read in two
different ways. First, it could be read: a strike by a labor union of employes of the
employer or a group of employes of the employer. The disjunctive could also be read as: a
strike by a labor union or group of employes of the employer.
"A statute is ambiguous if reasonable, well-informed persons could disagree as to its
meaning." Trinwith v. LIRC, 149 Wis. 2d 634, 642, 439 N.W.2d 581, 585 (Ct. App. 1989).
Section 108.04(10)(d) Stats. is subject to at least three interpretations. Under one
interpretation, a strike by any union is enough to disqualify the barring of employees from
being a "lock out". LIRC's interpretation would be that a strike by the employees' union,
regardless of the location and regardless of whether the employees were striking at their own
place of employment, would be enough to remove the barring of employees from the
definition of a "lock out." A third version would interpret that statute to mean that a strike
by the unionized employees would remove Illingworth' s actions from the definition of a
"lock out". Thus, the statute is ambiguous.
"A cardinal rule of statutory construction is that statutes must be construed to avoid
an absurd or unreasonable result." In Re P.A.K., 119 Wis. 2d 871, 881, 350 N.W.2d 677,
683 (1984) citing State v. Mendoza, 96 Wis. 2d 106, 115, 291 N.W.2d 478 (1980). In
seeking a reasonable interpretation of section 108.04(10)(d), one must keep in mind that by
enacting section 108.04 Stats., the legislature intended to protenct an employer from
financing a labor dispute in which it is a principal. De Leeuw v. DILHR, 71 Wis. 2d 446,
450, 238 N.W.2d 706, 709 (1976).
To interpret the statute to mean simply a labor union, without requiring a connection
7

to the employer or its employees, would lead to absurd results. Given this broad
construction, any union could go on strike and any employer could close the door on its
employes and claim that it did so directly subsequent to a strike by a union. The employer
could then claim that its barring of its employes would not constitute a lockout under section
108.04(10)(d). In this scenario the danger the legislature wished to prevent, an employer
financing a strike against it, is not even present. If some other company's employes go on
strike, there would be no way for an employer to finance that strike.
It would also be unreasonable to interpret the statute to say that the strike must have
been organized by a union to which the employer's employees belonged, but not require that
the employer's employees be involved. Otherwise, in theory, AFL-CIO employees in
Colorado could go on strike and any employer in Wisconsin whose employees belong to the
AFL-CIO could close their doors and claim that such action was not a lock-out under section
108.04(10)(d). Again, this is an overly broad interpretation, and again, there is no danger of
the Wisconsin employer of AFL-CIO workers financing the strike in Colorado.
The only reasonable interpretation of the statute would be to state that the disjunctive
language used in Section 108.04(10)(d) was merely used to distinguish between unionized
employees who strike and non-unionized employes who might go on strike. This
interpretation provides sufficient connection between the employer and employees where the
legislative intent is given purpose and is not defeated. It is more logical to permit employers
to close the door on its own employees whether the strike against it was orchestrated by the
employees union or whether it was organized by the employees themselves. Thus, the
employer is not forced to pay wages or unemployment compensation to those who are
8

striking against the employer.
Applying this interpretation of the statute, Illingworth's act of barring its employees
from reporting to work does, in fact, constitute a "lock out".
It is essentially undisputed by LIRC that the strike at CS&E did not constitute a labor
dispute at Illingworth. Instead, LIRC asserts that Illingworth's act of barring its employees
from reporting for work, in and of itself, constituted a labor dispute. The phrase "labor
dispute" is defined as "any controversy between an employer and the majority of the
employer's employes in a collective bargaining unit concerning the right or process or details
of collective bargaining or the designation or representatives. Any organization with which
either the employer or such majority is affiliated may be considered a party to the labor
dispute." Secs. 103.62(3), 111.02(9), 111.70(l)(g), 111.81(11), & 939.648(5)(a) Stats. The
act of barring employees from reporting to work is, in and of itself, a controversy. The
employees wish to work, the employers do not want the employees to report to work. Thus,
the first prong of section 108.04(10)(d) is satisfied.
The union to which Illingworth's employees belonged staged a strike at CS&E on
June 7, 1997. Four days later the Association instructed Illingworth to close it's doors to its
employees. Thus, Illingworth's conduct was directly subsequent to a strike, but not
subsequent to a strike against itself.
The strike was not orchestrated by Illingworth' s unionized employees. At no time
did Illingworth's employees who belonged to Local 18 promulgate a work stoppage at
Illingworth. Thus, Illingworth' s act of barring its employees from reporting to work was not
subsequent to a strike by its unionized employes, and thus, constituted a "lock out".
9

CONCLUSION AND ORDER
For all the foregoing reasons, it is the finding of this court that the strike at CS&E
was not a strike against either Illingworth or the Association. It is further determined that
Illingworth' s act of barring its employees from reporting to work did constitute a lock out
pursuant to section 108.04(10)(d), Stats.
THEREFORE, IT IS HEREBY ORDERED that the decision of the Labor and Industry
Review Commission is reversed and remanded for proceedings consistent with this decision.

title: LIRC Unemployment Insurance Decision — Thomas
text:
'.
STATE OF WISCONSIN CIRCUIT COURT LA CROSSE COUNTY •
BRANCH3
STANLEY G. THOMAS,
Plaintiff,
MEMORANDUM
v. DECISION AND ORDER
LABOR & INDUSTRY REVIEW
COM:MISSION, and THE STROH Case No. OO-CV-81 •
BREWERY CO., •
Defendants.
This case is before the court on plaintiff's appeal from a decision by the Labor and·
•I ndustry Review Commission ("LIRC") affirming a determination by th~ Unemployment
Compensation Division of the Department of Workforce Development that.denied benefits to the
plaintiff. Because the LIRC abused its discretion in a~rming the Unemployment Compensation
Division's denial of benefits to the plaintiff, the decision of the LIRC is reversed.
FACTS
P_laintiff, Stanley G. Thoma_s, began work for G. Heil~man Brewing in 1962. During the
past several years G. Heileman Brewing, or its assets, have been sold on several occasions, with
the assets most recently being owned by Stroh Brewing. Prior to August, 1999, Stroh Brewing
announced that it would be closing the La Crosse brewery and selling those assets. In the summer
of 1999, the New York investment firm Platinum Holdings purchased the brewery with the intent
-
.
to reopen the facility under the name of City Brewing Company. Both the City and County of La
Crosse agreed to loan money to City Brewing Company contingent upon the brewery having the
equivalent of 150 full time jobs when in final operation.
I

As part of the agreement,. the new purchasers would utili:z;e a somewhat modified .
collective bargaining agreement with the union which preserved the seniority rights akeady in
effect. Due to Mr. Thomas' 3 7 years of continuous employment with the brewery, he was
number two out of approximately 450 persons on the union seniority list. As it was Mr. Thomas'
reasonable expectation that he would be returned to his prior position, Mr. Thomas did not
conduct a work search under Wrs. STAT. § l 08. 04(2).
Because Mr. Thomas did not perform a work search and because Mr. Thomas did not
qualify for a waiver of the work search requirement, the Unemployment Compensation Division
denied his benefits. The testimony of Ms. Enerson indicates that a waiver was not granted
because Mr. Thomas was not "assured" of returning to work. Consequently, an Administrative
Law Judge affirmed the Unemployment Compensation Division's decision to deny benefits, which
1 Mr. Thomas appealed to the LIRC. The LIRC affirmed the decision of the Administrative Law
Judge, and now Mr. Thomas appeals to this court.
DISCUSSION
Under WIS. STAT.§ 102:23(1)(e), decisions of the commission may be set aside only if the
commission acted without or in excess of its powers, the order or award was procured by fraud,
or-the commission's findings of fact do not support the order or award. The LIRC sets forth the
requisite law regarding the overrulin~ of an administrative agency's decision. An agency's
interpretation will be sustained if it is merely reasonable. Harrtischfeger Corp. v. LIRC, 196 Wis.
2d 650, 661, 539 N.W.2d 98 (Wis. 1995). It will also be sustained even if an alternative
interpretation is equally reasonable (Id. at 663) or if an alternative interpretation is more
reasonable. UFE Inc. v. LIRC, 201 Wis. 2d 274,287, 548 N.W.2d 57 (Wis. 1996).
2

In addition, the Court agrees with theLIRC that "[a]n interpretation is unreasonable ifit
' ,
directly contravenes the words of the statute, ifit is clearly contrary to the legislative intent, or if
it is without a rational basis," Harnischfeger, at 662, However, the Court disagrees that the
LIRC's interpretation is reasonable and supported by a rational basis.
The LIRC's interpretation of the events directly contravenes the words of the statute,
namely that only a reasonable" expectation ofreemployment is required, not an "assured" or
"certain" expectation ofreemployment within 12 weeks. Also, it is clear that Mr. Thomas is the
type of individual committed to participation in the labor market. Mr. Thomas has participated in
the labor market for over 37 years and, in August of 1999, he had a reasonable expectation that
he would return to his same employment within 12 weeks. Mr, Thomas was not trying to
circumvent the system, he was following the law under DWD § 127.02(2) in that he would
receive a waiver of his work search requirement due to his personal circumstances.
Here, in determining that the LIRC acted in excess of its powers and that its findings of .
fact do not support the denial of benefits to Mr. Thomas, the Court looks to the applicable
statutes. Under the general qualifying requirements of WIS, STAT. § 108.04(2)(a) " ... a claimant
is eligible for benefits as to any given week for which he or she earns no wages only if
1. The individual is able to work and available for work and is seeking suitable work
during that week; and
2. As of that week the individual has registered for work."
These requirements may be waived under WIS.ADM.CODE§ DWD 127.02, which states:
"The Department may waive a claim and search for suitable work
requirement under s. DWD 127.01 for any week under any of the
following circumstances:
3

. (2) The Claimant has been laid off from work but has a
reasonable expect~tion of reemployment by an employer within
12 weeks after the week in which he or she appears at the public
employment office to initiate the benefit claim . . . . In
determining whether a claimant has a reasonable expectation of
re-employment, the Department shall consider factors including,
but not limited to, the following:
(a) The past history of!ayoffs and re-employments
by the employer; •
(b) Any information which the employer furnished
to the Claimant or the Department about the expected re
employment date; and
( c) Whether the Claimant has recall rights with the
employer under the provisions of any applicable collective
bargaining agreement.
(3) The claimant has a reasonable expectation of starting work
with a new employer within four weeks after the week in which he
or she appears at the public employment office to initiate the benefit
claim ... "
A waiver of the work search requirement should have been granted under DWD
§ 127.02(2), because the claimant need only meet the "reasonable" expectation ofreemployment
standard opposed to the "assured" or "certain" standard that the LIRC has incorrectly used to
deny benefits to Mr. Thomas. Ms. Enerson testified that "[t]here's a waiver up to a 12-week
period of time if you're assured you're going to be returning to work for a customary employer."
(DWD T. Hr' g. at 15 line 21 ). (Emphasis added). In failing to waive the work search
requirement for Mr. Thomas, the LIRC completely contravenes its own rule. The LIRC has
abused its discretion by implementing an "assured" or "certain" standard; the law states that a
"reasonable" expectation of reemployment is required. (Emphasis added).
In the summer of 1999, when the New York investment firm Platinum Holdings decided
to purchase Stroh Brewing (previously G. Heileman Brewery), there was a clear understanding,
made known to Mr. Thomas and all the other employees, on August 1, 1999, that Platinum
4

Holdings "would recall from the ,~urrent seniority list with the Stroh Brewery, in order on
•
seniority as soon as they could become operational in late September or early October." (DWD
T. Hr' g. at 12, line 20). Due to the fact that Mr. Thomas was number two out of 450 employees
on the seniority list, it is overwhelmingly reasonable for him to expect reemployment at his same
facility, doing the same work, under substantially the same collective bargaining agreement within
12 weeks.
In addition, the 12 week standard applies to Mr. Thomas' circumstances. Although, the
brewery changed ownership from G. Heileman, to other owners, to Stroh Brewing, and eventually
to City Brewery under Platinum Holdings, the 12 week standard is applicable and the work search
requirement should have been waived. First of all, Mr. Thomas has been continuously employed
at the same facility, doing the same job, under substantially the same collective bargaining
agreement (with recall rights) since 1962. Even though Mr. Thomas' paycheck would technically
come from a "new employer", his job location, his type of work, and his seniority status,
maintained over a 3 7-year period, were carried over to City Brewery. He did not have "new
employment"; for all intents and purposes, and in the spirit ofDWD § 127.02(2), Mr. Thomas
was going to return to work for his "customary employer".
The decisions of the DWD, the Administrative Law Judge, and the LIRC are totally
unsupported by a rational basis. Not only do the facts point to the granting of a work search
waiver for Mr. Thomas' personal circumstances, but the testimony of the LIB.C's only witness
does not shed light on how this determination was made. Basically, the LIRC "rubber-stamped"
the findings of the initial claims intake person without looking at the factual circumstances. This
is an abuse of power. At no time do any of the decision-making bodies, that denied benefits to
5

Mr. Thomas, render a well-reasQned, rational, or logical analysis on why the benefits were denied.
..
· _... -
''A discretionary determination, to be sustained, must demqnstrably be made
based upon the facts appearing in the record and in reliance on the appropriate
and applicable law. Additionally, and most importantly, a discretionary
determination must be the product of a rational mental process by which the
facts ofrecord and law relied upon are stated and are considered together with
the purpose of achieving a reasoned and reasonable determination." Hartung v.
Hartung, 102 Wis. 2d 58, 66, 306 N.W.2d 16 (Wi.s. 1981).
The LIRC did not properly apply its own regulations and did not give any reasons for its
decision. Because the decision of the LffiC is without a rational basis, the LffiC improperly
denied Mr. Thomas benefits by not granting him a waiver of the work search requirement under
DWD § 127.02(2).
ORDER
For the above stated reasons:
The decision of the LIRC is reversed.
Dated at La Crosse, Wisconsin, this &",lrclay of September, 2000.

title: LIRC Unemployment Insurance Decision — Nusberger
text:
STATE OF WISCONSIN CIRCUIT COURT MILWAUKEE COUNTY
DONALD L. NUSBERGER
Plaintiff,
CASE NO. 667-550
-vs-
MEMORANDUM DECISION
THE STATE OF WISCONSIN, LABOR AND
INDUSTRY REVIEW COMMISSION, and
SILVERSTEIN & HICKS, S.C.,
Defendants.
This is an action for judicial review pursuunt to
Sections 108.09(7) and 102.23(1) Wis. Stats. of a Labor and Industry
Review Commission decision denying the plaintiff unemployment
compensation benefits.
The plaintiff, Donald L. Nusberger, was employed
by the law firm of Silverstein & Hicks, s.c. as an investigator
and paralegal. He was initially employed by the law firm in
1976. His duties were that of an investigator, but over the
years his knowledge and skills increased to the point where he
functioned as a paralegal. By mid 1984 Nusberger did vlrtually
all of the firm's intake and initial contact with potential clients.
On July 5, 1984, Nusberger was discharged for alleged unauthorized
outside activities connected with the legal profession.
After a hearing, the following Findings of Pact and
Conclusions of Law were made which were ultimately afficmed by
the Commission:
-1-

In 1982 and again in the spring of 1984,
the employe had been informed by the employer
that he was not to engage in any outside
activities connected with the legal profession
without their authorization. That is a reasonable
requirement for a law firm to impose on its
employes to avoid any potential conflict
of interest.
The employer later became aware that
the employe had established some sort of
business relationship with another attorney.
Without the employer's knowledge or permission
he had worked on personal injury cases for
the other attorney. He had taken personal
injury forms belonging to the employer to
the offices of the other attorney. He informed
the employer that he intended to refer cases
to the other attorney that the employer did
not wish to handle.
Under the circumstances, the employe's
actions in engaging in outside business activities
connected with the legal profession without
the employer's authorization evinced a wilful,
intentional and substantial disregard for
-2-

the employer's interests and for the standards
of conduct that the employer had a right
to expect of him.
Sections 108.09(7) and 102.23(1) Stats. provide for
the judicial review of such findings and conclusions.
Section 102.23(l)(d) provides:
Upon such hearing, the Court may confirm or set
aside such order or award; and any judgment which
may theretofore have been rendered thereon; but
the same shall be set aside only upon the
following grounds:
1. That the commission acted without or in excess
of its powers.
2. That the order or award was procured by fraud.
3. That the findings of fact by the commission do
not support the order or award.
The plaintiff has submitted to the Court considerable
supplementary materials outside of the record. This Court cannot
consider those materials as this review is to be based upon the
record. Section 102.23(l)(c) Stats.
The test used by a Court in reviewing the sufficiency
of the evidence to support the findings is whether there is any
credible evidence in the record to support the finding made.
Under this test, a Court upon review will affirm the Findings
if there is any credible evidence to sustain those Findings.
It is the function of the Department and not the reviewing Court
to determine the credibility of evidence or witnesses and it
is for the Department to weigh the evidence and decide what should
be believed. Estex Packaging~ DILHR, 89 Wis. 2nd, 739 (1979).
-3-

The plaintiff in his reply brief contends that the
Findings should be set aside because fraud was involved. "Fraud"
to the effect that an order may be set aside only upon the ground
that it was procured by fraud means fraud of the Commission and
not fraud on the part of the parties or attorneys. Boles v.
Industrial Commission, 5 Wis. 2nd, 392 (1958). This Court is
satisfied that there is substantial credible evidence to support
the factual findings and therefore this Court. is bound by those
findings.
Section 108.04(5) Stats. provides that an employe
discharged for misconduct is to be denied unemployment compensation
benefits. The determination that an employe was discharged for
misconduct is a legal conclusion.
This Court is not bound by the Commission's determination
of a question of law, but the Court will not independently redetermine
every legal conclusion of the Commission. If several rules,
or applications of a rule, are equally consistent with the purpose
of a statute, the Court will accept the Commission's formulations
and application of the standards. Tecumseh Products Co. Y._:_ W.E.R.B.,
23 Wis. 2nd, 118, 126 N.W. 2nd, 520 (1964); Milwaukee Transformer
Co. v. Industrial Comm., 22 Wis. 2nd, 502, 126 N.W. 2nd, 6 (1964);
C.L. Cheese v. Industrial Comm., 21 Wis. 2nd, 8, 123 N.W. 2nd,
553 (1963).
-4-

The case of Boynton Cab 9.£.:._ .Y.!_ Neubeck, 237 Wis.
249 (1941) discussed the factors to be considered in determining
misconduct under Section 108.04(5) Stats. The Court set down
four separate basis for concluding that an employe's conduct
was misconduct under the statute. These four are: (1) conduct
evincing such wilful or wanton disregard of an employer's interests
as found in deliberate violations of standards of behavior which
the employer has the right to expect of his employe, (2) conduct
evincing carelessness or negligence of such degree or recurrence
as to manifest equal culpability, wrongful intent or evil design,
(3) conduct showing an intentional and substantial disregard
of the employer's interests and (4) conduct showing an intentional
and substantial disregard of the employe•s duties and obligations
to his employer.
The Commission has concluded that the employe Nusberger's
actions evinced a wilful, intentional, and substantial disregard
for the employer's interests and for the standards of conduct
that the employer had a right to expect of him. Given the factual
determinations which this Court is bound by, this Court must
necessarily agree: and, therefore, the decision of the Commission
is affirmed.
Dated at Milwaukee, Wisconsin, this 14th day of February, 198E

The commission modifies and, as modified, affirms in part and reverses in part the
appeal tribunal decision. Accordingly, the claimant is eligible for Pandemic
Unemployment Assistance (PUA) under section 2102(a)(3)(A)(ii)(I)(kk) of the CARES
Act for weeks 13 through 20 of 2020, if otherwise qualified.
By the Commission: /s/

1 Appeal Rights: See the blue enclosure for the time limit and procedures for obtaining judicial
review of this decision. If you seek judicial review, you must name the following as defendants in the
summons and the complaint: the Labor and Industry Review Commission, all other parties in the
caption of this decision or order (the boxed section above), and the Department of Workforce
Development. Appeal rights and answers to frequently asked questions about appealing an
unemployment insurance decision to circuit court are also available on the commission’s website,
http://lirc.wisconsin.gov.

Procedural Posture
This case is before the commission to consider the claimant’s eligibility for
Pandemic Unemployment Assistance (PUA). An administrative law judge (ALJ) of
the Unemployment Insurance Division of the Department of Workforce
Development held a hearing and issued a decision. The commission received a
timely petition for review. The commission has considered the petition, and it has
reviewed the evidence submitted at the hearing.
Findings of Fact and Conclusions of Law
1. The claimant was last employed on March 18, 2020 (week 12). She was self-
employed as a part-time cleaner for two apartment complexes.
2. The claimant worked 22 to 25 hours per week, because her plan was to go to
part-time retirement January 1, 2020. She only worked as much as she could
without her pay adversely affecting how much she receives in Social Security
benefits.
3. The claimant does not have a medical reason as to why she did not work more
than 25 hours per week.
4. On March 12, 2020 (week 11), Governor Evers issued Executive Order #72, in
which he declared that a public health emergency exists in the state due to the
spread of COVID-19. All state agencies were ordered to assist in the response
to the public emergency.
5. On March 13, 2020, Governor Evers directed the Department of Health
Services Secretary-designee Andrea Palm to issue an order mandating
statewide closure of all public and private schools effective at 5 p.m. on March
18 (week 12).
6. On March 18, 2020 (week 12), Governor Evers issued Emergency Order #7,
which modified the eligibility requirements for individuals seeking
unemployment insurance benefits during the COVID-19 pandemic concerning
their ability to work, availability for work, and obligation to search for work.
7. On March 24, 2020 (week 13), the state issued a Safer at Home Order,
Emergency Order #12. All individuals in Wisconsin were ordered to stay at
home, with outlined exceptions. All non-essential businesses and operations
were ordered to cease all activities, except for minimum basic operations and
operations where employees could work from home. All essential businesses
and operations were encouraged to remain open. On April 25, 2020 (week 17),
the state’s second Safer at Home Order, Emergency Order #28, went into effect
upon the expiration of the first.
8. The primary place at which the claimant cleaned was shut down when the first
Safer at Home Order was issued in week 13 of 2020.
9. On Saturday, May 9, 2020 (week 19), the Department of Workforce
Development issued an emergency rule pertaining to the requirements for
individuals seeking unemployment insurance benefits during the COVID-19
2
Theresa A Aronson
20405108MD

pandemic with respect to an individual’s ability to work, availability for work,
and obligation to search for work. These rules supplanted Emergency Order #7,
which went into effect in week 12 of 2020. The new rule is applied beginning
with week 20 of 2020.
10. On Wednesday, May 13, 2020 (week 20), the Wisconsin Supreme Court struck
down the second Safer at Home Order, invalidating all provisions other than
mandated school closures.
11. The claimant was unable to return to work in May 2020, because she was
home-schooling her two grandchildren while their father worked.
12. The claimant was eligible for PUA for weeks 13 through 20 of 2020, if
otherwise qualified.
Memorandum Opinion
As a general rule, to be eligible for unemployment insurance benefits as to any
given week, a claimant must be able to work, available for work, and actively
seeking work during the week.2 “Able to work” means that the claimant maintains
an attachment to the labor market and has the physical and psychological ability to
engage in some substantial gainful employment in suitable work.3 “Available for
work” means that the claimant maintains an attachment to the labor market and is
ready to perform full-time suitable work in the labor market.4 “Full-time work”
means work performed for 32 hours or more per week.5 However, an individual with
a physical or psychological restriction will not be considered unavailable for work
solely because of his or her inability to work full-time, provided the individual is
available for suitable work for the number of hours the individual is able to work.6
A claimant is not available for suitable work if he or she has withdrawn from the
labor market due to restrictions on his or her availability for work.7 Suitable work is
defined as work that is reasonable considering the claimant’s training, experience,
and duration of unemployment as well as the availability of jobs in the labor
market.8
The unemployment insurance program is intended to provide temporary wage
insurance for individuals who are able to work and available for work but are
unemployed by reason of lack of suitable work. The able to work, available for work,
and actively seeking work requirements implement this design by testing whether
the fact that an individual did not work for any week was involuntary due to the
unavailability of suitable work.9
2 Wis. Stat. § 108.04(2)(a).
3 Wis. Admin. Code § DWD 128.01(3)(a).
4 Wis. Admin. Code § DWD 128.01(4)(a).
5 Wis. Stat. § 108.02(15s).
6 Wis. Admin. Code § DWD 128.01(4)(a).
7 Wis. Admin. Code § DWD 128.01(4)(a).
8 Wis. Admin. Code § DWD 100.02 (61).
9 UIPL No. 10-20, p. 3.
3
Theresa A Aronson
20405108MD

As a self-employed individual, the claimant is not eligible for regular unemployment
insurance benefits, but Section 2102 of the Coronavirus Aid, Relief, and Economic
Security (CARES) Act of 2020 created a new temporary federal program, Pandemic
Unemployment Assistance (PUA), that provides benefits to some self-employed
individuals, if they meet the definition of a “covered individual.” A “covered
individual” is someone who meets each of the following three conditions:
Condition #1: The individual is not eligible for regular unemployment
compensation (UC), extended benefits (EB), or pandemic emergency unemployment
compensation (PEUC). This includes an individual who has exhausted all rights to
such benefits, as well as an individual who is self-employed, seeking part-time
employment, lacking sufficient work history, or who is otherwise not qualified for
regular UC, EB, or PEUC. Self-employed individuals include independent
contractors and gig economy workers.
Condition #2: The individual must self-certify that he or she is otherwise able
and available to work within the meaning of applicable state law, except that the
individual is unemployed, partially unemployed, or unable or unavailable to work
because of a listed COVID-19 reason in Section 2102(a)(3)(A)(ii) of the CARES Act.
Condition #3: The individual must provide required documentation
substantiating employment or self-employment or the planned commencement of
employment or self-employment.10
The issue in this case is whether the claimant is a “covered individual” as of week
13 of 2020.
The claimant satisfied Conditions #1 and 3. She was self-employed in a cleaning
business and provided the required documentation to prove her self-employment.
The claimant also satisfied Condition #2, but only in weeks 13 through 20 of 2020,
while the complex where she cleaned was closed due to COVID-19 and the Safer at
Home Orders were in effect.
To be eligible for unemployment insurance benefits as to any given week, a
claimant must be able to work, available for work, and actively seeking work during
the week.11 “Able to work” means that the claimant maintains an attachment to the
labor market and has the physical and psychological ability to engage in some
substantial gainful employment in suitable work.12 “Available for work” means that
the claimant maintains an attachment to the labor market and is ready to perform
full-time suitable work in the labor market.13 “Full-time work” means work
performed for 32 hours or more per week.14 The claimant had voluntarily restricted
herself to part-time employment to maximize her Social Security benefits and was
10 UIPL No. 16-20, Change 4, Attachment I, p. 4.
11 Wis. Stat. § 108.04(2)(a).
12 Wis. Admin. Code § DWD 128.01(3)(a).
13 Wis. Admin. Code § DWD 128.01(4)(a).
14 Wis. Stat. § 108.02(15s).
4
Theresa A Aronson
20405108MD

thus not available for full-time work, a requirement for unemployment benefits.
However, in weeks 13 through 20 of 2020, the department was required to consider
a claimant to be available for suitable work during a public health emergency if the
claimant was quarantined under local, state or federal government direction or
guidance.
The government quarantine ended in week 20, so the claimant could have returned
to her self-employment in week 21 of 2020. She did not return to her self-
employment in that week, because she was homeschooling her grandchildren –
another restriction on her availability for full-time work. While there is a provision
regarding home-schooling children whose schools are closed – section
2102(a)(3)(A)(ii)(I)(dd) of the CARES Act – that section applies to an individual who
has primary caregiving responsibility for a child in their household. The claimant’s
grandchildren resided with their father.
So, the claimant was eligible for PUA under section 2102(a)(3)(A)(ii)(I)(kk) of the
CARES Act, which is applicable to a self-employed worker who experienced a
significant diminution of her customary or usual services because of the COVID-19
public health emergency, for weeks 13 through 20 of 2020. As of week 21 of 2020,
the claimant could not certify that she was otherwise able and available to work
within the meaning of applicable state law, except that she was unemployed,
partially unemployed, or unable or unavailable to work because of a listed COVID-
19 reason. A claimant ceases to be eligible for PUA when she no longer meets the
requirements to be a covered individual.

text:
STATE OF WISCONSIN CIRCUIT COURT BROWN COUNTY
BRANCH V
ALTON A. ANSCHUTZ,
Plaintiff,
vs. Case No. 93-CV-616
STATE OF WISCONSIN, DEPARTMENT OF
INDUSTRY, LABOR AND HUMAN RELATIONS
UNEMPLOYMENT COMPENSATION DMSION AUTHENTICATED COPY
FIL 1:0
(In re the account of Moorehead
Machinery and Boiler Co.),
AUG 2 S1 993
Defendant.
LYNN VERHEYEN
CLERK OF COURTS
BROWN COUNTY. WI
DECISION ON MOTION TO DISMISS THE COMPLAINT
FACTS
The plaintiff is seeking judicial review of a Labor and Industry Review Commission
(hereinafter, Commission) finding that he failed to pursue a job opening that was made known
to him by a public agency and as a result he was overpaid $727 in unemployment
compensation. The Commission affirmed the Department administrative law judge's finding
that he was to repay the overpaid unemployment compensation. The Commission mailed the
plaintiff a copy of the decision on April 2, 1993. The plaintiff served a summons and
complaint upon the Office of the Secretary of the Department of Industry, Labor and Human
Relations on May 3, 1993. They were then given to the Enforcements Section of the Bureau
of Legal Affairs on May 4, 1993. The summons and complaint. were received by the
Commission on May 5, 1993.

DECISION
Failure to Name the Proper Parties as Defendants
Actions for judicial review of the Commission's decisions are controlled by Wisconsin
Administrative Code LIRC 2.05. This section states that any judicial review shall be conducted
according to the procedure outlined in Wisconsin Statutes sections 108.09(7), and 102,23 which
states that the Commission and the adverse party shall be made defendants. The plaintiff failed
to name both the Commission and Moorehead Machinery and Boiler Company as defendants
in the complaint's caption. The S\lpreme Court of Wisconsin, however, held that "a caption
is not a part of a pleading and the nature of an action must be determined from the allegations
of a pleading rather than its caption." Nigbor v DILHR 120 Wis.2d 375, 381 (1984) citing
Lees v. ILHR Department, 49 Wis.2d 491,496 (1971). Thus, not naming parties as defendants
in the caption is a "hypertechnical error" which does not deprive the court of jurisdiction. Id.
at 382.
The complaint describes the plaintiffs claim with the Commission in allegations four
through six. Allegation seven states that the plaintiff seeks to reverse the Commission's last
finding. Allegation eight alleges a basis in law and fact for reversing the Commission's
findings. All of these allegations show ti\at the complaint is again.st the Com1-nission and not
Department of Industry, Labor and Human Relations. Therefore, failing to. name the proper
parties in the caption is not grounds to dismiss the complaint.
Failure to Serve the Commission within the Statutory Period
Wis. Stat. §§102.23(l)(a) and 108.90(7)(a) state that the summons and complaint must
2

be served upon the Commission within 30 days after the date that the Commission's order is
mailed to the party's last-known address. Section 102.23(l)(b) and Wis. Admin. Code LIRC
2.05 state that the summons and complaint must be served upon a commissioner or agent
authorized by the Commission to accept service. The Commission's decision which was
mailed to the plaintiff on April 2, 1993 also included an enclosure stating the above
information and the address and room number where they could be served.
It is settled in Wisconsin that "the failure to serve necessary parties within the statutory
period ... is an irremediable defect." Gomez v. LIRC, 153 Wis.2d 686 (1989) quoting Cruz v.
IHLR Department, 81 Wis.2d 442, 448 (1978). Because the statutes detailing proper service
must be strictly followed, the failure to serve necessary parties is an error which deprives the
court of jurisdiction. Id. at 692.
In Gomez, the plaintiff sought judicial review of a Labor and Industry Review
Commission decision. The plaintiff served the summons and complaint upon a receptionist of
an agency which was related to, but legally separate from the Commission. The Commission •
did not receive the summons and complaint within the statutory_ period. This deprived the
court of jurisdiction. Id.
Mr. Anschutz also served the summons and complaint upon an agency that is related
to, but legally separate from the Commission. The Commission also did not receive the
summons and complaint until after the statutory period had elapsed. Mr. Anschutz' s factual
circumstances are the san1e as those in Gomez, except that Mr. Gomez's claim involved
worker's compensation, not unemployment compensation.
Therefore, as Mr. Anschutz failed to properly serve the summons and complaint within
3

the statutorily prescribed period, and such a mistake deprives this court of jurisdiction under •
Gomez, the plaintiffs complaint must be dismissed.
Dated in Green Bay, Wisconsin, thisd(Jlay of August 1993.
