title: LIRC Unemployment Insurance Decision — Kimball
text:
STATE OF WISCONSIN IN CIRCUIT COURT DANE COUNTY
* * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * *
#131-176
SCOTT C. KIMBALL, *
Plaintiff,
* MEMORANDUM
-vs-
DECISION
COMMISSIONERS FOR THE *
DEPARTMENT OF INDUSTRY,
LABOR & HUMAN RELATIONS
and OLIN MATHIASON CORP., *
Defendants ..
* * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * -* * * *· * *
This review action is concerned with the claim of plaintiff Scott C. Kimball (here
after" Scott") for unemployment compensation benefits arising from the termina
tion of his employment on January 23, 1970, with the OJ.in Corporation (described
as Olin..cMathiason Corporation in the title of this action). The facts hereinafter
set forth are those brought out at the hearing held June 2, 1970, before the appeal
tribunal.
As of the termination of employment Scott was 19 years old and had been employed
by the Olin Corporation for about nine months at the Badger Ordinance plant near
Baraboo. The crucial facts are succinctly set forth in Exhibit 1, which is Scott's
signed statement dated February 23, 1970, which is on a printed form bearing
the heading "EMPLOYE STATEMENT -- U. C. CLAIM INVESTIGATION." It is
the Court's understanding that this signed statement was furnished in connection
with the preliminary investigation made of Scott's claim for unemployment com
pensation benefits prior to the department deputy's initial determination that Scott
was ineligible for benefits. This statement read:
"I was employed by the above employer as wringerman for a period
of about 9 months until January 23, 1970.
"I had made application with the Technical School in Madison,
Wisconsin to attend school the second semester. Registration was
to take place on January 23, 1970. On about January 13, 1970, I
told my supervisor, Carl Schultz, that I would probably go to school
on about January 23, 1970. He said that he'd get the papers lined
up for me to sign and so that I'd be able. to clean out my locker. I
said that would be O, K.
1

"On January 17, 1970 I received notice from the Technical School that
I wouldn't be accepted for that semester. I would have to wait until
the next semester started. On the 19th I told Carl Schultz about it
and he said he would try to stop the papers from_ going through so
that I could continue working. On the 21st I was advised that the
paper work regarding my termination had already gone through and
nothing could be done about it. I was then terminated on January 23,
1970."
Scott's testimony at the hearing did not contradict or repudiate any portion of his
above quoted statement. He testified that he received the notice from the Madison
Technical School that he would not be accepted for the second semester of 1970
on Saturday, January 17th, when he was off work for the weekend, and took it to
work with him on Monday, January 19th and gave it to his s-upervisor., Carl Schultz.
Schultz "said he was going to call the front office and try to stop the termination if
possible." (Emphasis added.) Scott was further asked these questions a:nd gave
these answers (Tr. 10-11):
"Q Apparently Mr. Schultz didn't say anything to you about stop
ping your employment other than he wasn't able to stop this
termination?
"A He said he was going to try. That is all he could do.
"Q So when Friday came around you were done. He said you
didn't have any opportunity to continue?
"A He told me Wednesday that it couldn't be stopped and that
Friday was my last day."
In the presentation of Scott's position at the hearing before this Court it was con
tended that Schultz had agreed to Scott's attempted rescission of his notice of
termination. The above quoted portions of the record, however, makes it clear
"lfi'
that Schultz did not so agree but only stated that he would to stop the ter
mination papers going through.
The appeal tribunal in the findings of fact portion of its decision of June 11, 1970,
which affirmed the deputy's initial determination and held that Scott was ineligible
for benefits, found:
"On or about January 13, 1970, the employe informed his supervisor
that he would probably leave work in order to attend school the second
semester and that registration would take place about January 23. The
supervisor then suggested that termination papers be prepared for his
signature and he agreed.
2

"On January 17 the employe received notice that he would not be
accepted at the school for the second semester. On January 19 he
informed his supervisor that he would be unable to attend school.
The supervisor agreed to attempt to stop the processing of his ter
mination papers so that he could continue at work. Two days later
. he was notified that such processing could not be stopped and that
January 23 would be his last day of work. •
"The employe contends that he did not terminate his employment.
However, he had notified his supervisor of his probable intent to
leave his employment on January 23 and had agreed that termination
papers should be processed accordingly. Although he changed his
mind upon learning that he would be unable to attend school and
informed the employer of his changed intention, the employer did
not agree to a withdrawal of his notice of intent to quit. Therefore,
the termination of his employment resulted because of his notice to
the employer of his intention to leave his employment on January 23,
rather than because of any action initiated by the employer. •
"The appeal tribunal therefore finds that in week 4 of 1970 the
employe terminated his employment, within the meaning of section
108. 04 (7) (a) of the statutes, and that such termination was not
within any of the exceptions to said section."
The summary of the material evidence previously set forth herein amply supports
the above quoted findings of fact. Two cases involving a quitting and an attempted
. rescinding of such quitting have been decided by the Circuit Court for Dane County:
Shallock v. Ind, Comm. (January 28, 1958) and Powers v. Ind. Comm. (1967, Case
No. 119-483). In both cases it was held that the quitting was final which is in •
accord with this Court's understanding of the law. Therefore, the Court has no
alternative, but to confirm the department's order of July 16, 1970, which affirmed
the appeal tribunal's decision.
The testimony discloses that, if Scott had been permitted to rescind his notice of
termination, he would have had only five more days of employment before he would
have been laid off because the department he was employed in then closed down.
The number of employees then laid off is not mentioned in the testimony, but in
the presentation to this Court it was stated that approximately 200 were so dis
charged. It is a fair inference that the pending layoff was the reason for the
employer refusiq.g to permit Scott to withdraw his notice of termination. The
Court sympathizes with Scott's feeling of being unjustly treated because these 200
or so other employees received unemployment compensation benefits while he did
not.
With the consent of counsel for the department and the court, the presentation of
Scott's position before the court was.made by his father. In this presentation the
father stated that he knew of a number of instances in which employees at the
3

Badger Ordinance plant had given notice to quit and then had been pennitted to
continue their employment after changing their minds. If this had been presented
as testimony at the hearing before the appeal tribunal, which it was not, it could
well have supported a finding of a general practice on the part of Olin to pennit
employees to rescind their notices of tennination. This Court, however, is pre
cluded from considering this because it is not in the record. Inasmuch as the
evidence supports the finding of fact of the appeal tribunal, the Court has no power
. under the statutes to remand the case for taking further evidence.
Let judgment be entered confirming the department's order of July 16, 1970.
Dated this 11th day of May, 1971.
/s/ George R. Currie
· RESERVE CIRCUIT JUDGE

text:
STATE OF WISCONSIN CIRCUIT COURT DANE COUNTY
* * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * *
*
JOHN STRANGE PAPERBOARD DIVISION *
of The Menasha Corporation, *
* MEMORANDUM DECISION
Plaintiff, *
* CASE NO. 134-236
vs. *
*
*
DEPARTMENT OF INDUSTRY, LABOR
AND HUMAN RELATIONS and *
*
ROBERT PARDEE,
*
*
Defendants.
*
* * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * *
Before Hon. George R. Currie, Reserve Circuit Judge
* * * * * * *·* * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * *
This is an action to review a decision of the defendant department dated
August 5, 1971, which held that on November 16, 1970, the defendant employee Rober~
Pardee terminated his employment with the plaintiff employer with good cause·attrib
utable to the employer within the meaning of sec. l08.04(7)(b), Stats., and was
eligible for unemployment compensation benefits based on his employment with the
employer. The department's deputy had made an initial determination that Pardee was
ineligible for benefits. On appeal Examiner Reed acting in the capacity of an Appeal
Tribunal, reached the same conclusion and found that Pardee's quitting his employ
ment was not with good cause attributable to the employer by decision dated llay 6,
1971. The department's decision here under review reversed the decision by the
Appeal Tribunal.
Pardee entered the employ of the emp::.oyer on April 29, 1963, as a draftsman in
the engineering department. At that time Ron Harvey, the chief engineer, was in
charge of the department which had two draftsmen. The employer was engaged in the
manufacture of paper and paper products, but it also manufactured for its own use
papermaking machinery and developments in such machinery, and the drawings produced
by Pardee were design drawings for this and also of new products.
Bruce Stevens became shop manager in 1968 and in 1969 was also put in charge
of the engineering department in which Pardee worked and Harvey was transferred
from the engineering department to the sales department. It was also in 1969 that
Pardee was made chief draftsman.
In the summer of 1967 the employer had adopted a new policy of having all of
its employees sign the following form of agreement:
In consideration of my continued employment by John Strange Paper
Company or by one of your subsidiary or affiliated corporations and the
compensation paid for my services, I will treat as for your sole
benefit, and fully and promptly disclose and assign to you without
additional compensation, all works of art, ideas, discoveries, irr-ren:t:iono
APPENDIX B

and improvements, which, while I an: so employed, are made, conceived
or reduced to practice by me, alone or with others, during or after
usual working ·hours either on or off my job, and which are related to
your business or interests or which result from tasks assigned to me
by you.
I agree at your exper.se, at any time during or after such employ
ment, to sign all papers and do such other acts and things as you deem
necessary or desirable and may reasonably require of me to protect your
rights to said works of art, ideas, discoveries, inventions and improve
ments, including applying for, obtaining, and enforcing copyrights and
patents on said work of art, discoveries, inventions, and improvements in
any and all countries.
During and after such employment, I will not divulge or appropriate
to my own use or to the use of others, except as you authorize or direct,
any secret or confidential information or knowledge obtained by me during
such employment, except as such information or knowledge shall be made
public by you or by others not deriving such information or knowledge
from you.
Counting employees of subsidiary companies, the employer had over 200 employees.
Later upon checking it was found that approximately 30 or 35 employees had been over
looked for various reasons in obtaining these agreements, including Pardee. In
September or October, 1970, Pardee was told he would have to sign such an agreement
(Tr. 22, 31). This occurred at the first of two conferences held with Pardee by
Stevens and Gschwind, the latter apparently being Stevena's superior, (Tr, 16, 31).
The second conference took place on either November 12 or 13, 1970 (Tr. 31). It
was at this second conference when Pardee was handed a letter signed by Stevens
(Ex. 2) which stated that if Pardee had not signed the agreement by 8 :00 a.m. of
November 16, 1970, his employment with the employer would be terminated as of that
date (Tr. 7).
Pardee reported for work at 8:00 a.m. on Nonday, November 16, 1970, his usual
starting time (Tr, 38). He asked Stevens if he still had to sign the agreement to
maintain his job and Stevens told him he did (Tr. 8). He then left the plant (Tr. 8)
and subsequently filed for unemployment compensation benefits,
The decision of the department of August 5, 1971, contains the following
findings of fact:
"The employe worked for the employer, a paper manufacturing
company, about eight years as a draftsman. His last day of work
was November 13, 1970,
"In July of 1967 the employer adopted a policy requiring each
of its more than 200 employes to sign the following agreement:"
(The text of the agreement was here set forth verbatim.)
"Although the employe did not sign the agreement in 1967, he
continued working and the matter was not discussed with him until
September or October of 1970 when he was requested to sign it. He
was subsequently told that unless he signed the agreement, his employ
ment would be terminated, The employe objected to signing the agreement
-2-

because he believed that, inview of changes which had occurred in
the department in 1969 and 1970, his employment WO!fld be terminated
after he had signed it. He also was concerned about the effect of
the third paragraph of the agreement upon his securing future employ
ment as a draftsman.
"On November 12, 1970, the employe was notified in writing that
if he did not deliver a signed copy of the agreement to his supervisor
by 8:00 a.m. on November 16, 1970, his employment would be terminated.
On November 16 he reported for work but was again advised that it was
necessary that he sign the agreement. He refused to do so and left
the employer's establishment.
"Although the employe alleged that he was discharged, he had
alternative of signing the agreement and continuing the employment
relationship or refusing to sign it and thereby discontinuing the
employment relationship. His refusal to sign the agreement con-·
stituted a quitting of his employment.
"The requirement that the employe sign the agreement was un
reasonable and he was justified in quitting.
"The commission therefore finds that in week 47 of 1970 the
employe terminated his employment with good cause attributable to
the employer, within the meaning of section 108.04(7)(b) of the
statutes."
One comment should be made with respect to the statement in the findings,
"Although the employe did not sign the agreement in 1967,. . " There is no testi
mony that Pardee was ever asked to sign such an agreement in 1967, and he testified
he was unaware any other employees had signed such agreement in 1967 (Tr. 27).
Pardee testified that he told Gschwind and Stevens that he could agree with the
first and second paragraphs of the requested agreement and it was only the third
paragraph to which he objected (Tr. 34). Thus we are here concerned with only the
reasonableness of the third paragraph which prohibited him from divulging secret or
confidential information obtained during his employment by the employer.
There is no question but that as chief draftsman Pardee was in a sensitive
position. The principal way that one paper manufacturer can make paper different
than that of its competitors is by use of different machinery. As chief draftsman
making drawings of papermaking machines or developments therein Pardee would have
knowledge of any secret methods entering into the design thereof. This secret in
formation in the nature of the employer's trade secrets in the hands of a competitor
could be used to harm the employer's business.
Whether protection is based on property or confidential relationship, it is
clear that even without an agreement such as requested of Pardee in this. instance,
employees may not lawfully disclose to third parties secret and confidential in
formation gained from their employment. Kreider, "Trends in the Enforcement of
Restrictive Employment Contracts," (1966) 35 University of Cincinnati Law Review 16;
Anno. 165 A.L,R. 1453, 1454; Anno. 30 A.L,R. 3rd 631; Milgrim on Trade Secrets, sec.
1.09; Restatement of Torts sec. 757; Forest Laboratories, Inc. v, Formulations, Inc.
(D.C. Wis, 1969), 299 F. Supp. 202; Bull v. Log Etronics, Inc. (D.C. Va. 1970), 323
F. Supp. 115.
-3-

Inasmuch as Pardee was under a legal duty not to disclose to others the trade
secrets of his employer obtained through his employmen1;, there is nothing unreason
able in the empioye requiring that his legal duty be set forth in a written agree
ment. A reading of the third paragraph of the requested agreement discloses nothing
unreasonable in its provisions.
That the present agreement does not differ in any material respect from other
non-disclosure agreements made throughout the commercial community is evident from
the suggested forms listed in Milgrim on Trade Secrets 3.05 (2) and 8 Am. Jur. Legal
Forms "Master and Servant" 8 :1312-1316. Many of the forms listed are similar in
scope, and all appear to permit the limited non-disclosure agreement required in the
present situation.
Counsel for the department in the hearing before this Court contended that what
the department held was not that requiring non-disclosure of trade secret agreements
from the employees in a sensitive position such as Pardee were unreasonable generally,
but that it was unreasonable under the particular facts of this case; If this is
the basis of the department's decision, it is not apparent from the reading of it.
Assuming that counsel is correct in this contention, it is necessary to examine
closely the facts stated in the department's findings of fact to ascertain if there
is anything therein which would reasonably support the ultimate conclusion of the
department that requiring the agreement under such circumstances afforded Pardee
good cause attributable to the employer for quitting his employment.
The Court is satisfied that such circumstances necessarily are confined to
these two sentences of the department's findings:
" ... The employe objected to signing the agreement because
he believed that, in view of changes which had occurred in the
department in 1969 and 1970, his employment would be terminated
after he had signed it. He also was concerned about the effect
of the third paragraph of the agreement upon his securing future
employment as a draftsman."
The first reason given by Pardee, as found by the department, for objecting to
signing the agreement was that in view of changes which occurred in the engineering
department in 1969 and 1970 he was fearful that his employment would be terminated
after he signed the agreement. The record discloses that these changes had three
facets. The first was the transfer of chief engineer Harvey out of the department
and giving him a different kind of employment when the engineering department was
placed under Steven's supervision. (Tr. 14, 28). The second was the quitting (not
discharge) of the other draftsman (Tr. 14, 28), and the replacement of such drafts
man by a girl who had no experience in drafting (Tr. 29). However, she did under
take training in drafting by attending a course in drafting at the vocational school
one night a week for six months (Tr. 37-38). The third was that most of the new
equipment design was being done outside the engineering office and a separate
drawing file was kept to which he had no access (Tr. 29). Stevens explained this
in his testimony that he had made product.ion drawings, as he had done in the past,
which were kept in his own file which were available wh~n needed, and that this was
separate from the work done by Pardee and his assistant (Tr. 15-16).
In any event, it was only a surmise on Pardee's part that his services would
no longer be needed and the employer had done nothing unreasonable upon which Pardee
-4-

grounded this surmise. Such surmise, therefore, was not good cause attributable to
the employer which· would justify him in quitting his job rather than signing the
agreement. Furthermore, it is immaterial whether or not Pardee 1 s fear of having his
employment terminated was justified. Signin:g the agreement would not hasten such
termination and, so long as he remained on the payroll, it was not unreasonable for
the employer to require the signing of the agreement.
The second reason advanced by Pardee, as found by the department, for him
refusing to sign the agreement was his concern as to the effect of the third para
graph upon securing future employment as a draftsman. Pardee did not directly
testify that he feared the third paragraph would prevent his obtaining further
employment, but this can be inferred from tuo bits of testimony he gave, One was
his asking Gschwind and Stevens "what they would call confidential material" (Tr,
34). The other was the advice he received from his attorney when Pardee submitted
the agreement to such attorney prior to November 16, 1970, and the attorney stated
it could '!muddy the water" which Pardee interpreted to mean would be. "an incon
venience" (Tr. 44), However, Pardee admitted he had signed a similar agreement
when he worked for the employer by whom he was employed prior to working for the
plaintiff which did not preclude him from obtaining employment by the plaintiff
(Tr, 35), He further admitted that the language of this prior agreement was sub
stantially the same as the agreement he refused to sign for the plaintiff employer
(Tr. 35).
Counsel for the· department relies upon Pardee' s testimony that, when he asked
Gschwind and Stevens what they would call confidential material, "They would not.
or could not tell me (Tr. 34). However, he had signed a similar agreement worded
substantially the same for a prior employer, and had consulted his own attorney con
cerning the agreement and presumably had that attorney's advice as to uhat the third
paragraph meant before he quit his job on November 16, 1970. Moreover, because the
third paragraph is so simply and clearly worded as to merely set forth the legal
duty Pardee was already under not to disclose secret or confidential information,
his own fear that it might jeopardize his future employment as a draftsman could
not as a matter of law be the basis of a finding of £act that he quit his employment
£or good cause attributable to his employer,
In Kessler v. Industrial Comm. (1965), 27 !vis. 2d 398, 401, 134 N.W. 2d 398,
the Wisconsin Supreme Court in attempting to define what good cause attributable
to the employer means as used in sec. 108.04(7)(b), Stats., as follows:
"Good cause attributable to the employer as distinguished
from discharge must involve some fault on its part and must be
real and substantial. 11
The basis of this Court's decision in the instant case is that as a matter of
law the record here does not establish any real and substantial fault on the part of
the employer. The credible evidence presented here simply will not support a
finding that Pardee's quitting his employment rather than signing the agreement was
due to a good cause attributable to the employer.
-s-

Let judgment be entered reversing t~e departlilent'~ decision of August 5, 1971,
with directions to affirm the Appeal Tri~unal's decision of May 6, 1971.
Dated this 20th day of July, 1972.
/s/ George R. Currie
Reserve Circuit Judge

Before Hon. Richard W. Bardwell, Judge
This is an action to review a decision of the Industrial Commission,
dated November 25, 1966, affirming a decision of an appeal tribunal. The
decision held that Margaret B. Berger, failed, without good cause, to accept
work offered her in week 33 of 1966, within the meaning of ss. 108.04(8)(a)
and (d) of the statutes, and that her eligibility for unemployment benefits was
suspended begining with week 33 of 1966 and until she has been employed
within at least four weeks and has earned wages equalling at least four
times her weekly benefit rate.
The plaintiff (hereinafter referred to as applicant) was laid off by
· y
the defendant, the Great Atlantic & Pacific Tea Co., Inc. (here-inafter re-
ferred to as the employer), on May 13, 1966 (in week 20), when the employer
discontinued operating the bakery in which applicant had been employed.
At the time of her layoff, applicant was paid three weeks' vacation pay and
~fnd one-half weeks' severance pay.
, .. , Applicant registered for work at a public employment office on May 31,
~
1966 (week 23). When she initiated her claim for unemployment benefits,
she was told by a representative of the Unemployment Compensation Depart
ment that because of her receipt of vacation and severance pay she would
not be eligible for unemployment benefits until after the period for which
she received vacation and severance payments had expired. She did not
register for work or claim unemployment benefits in weeks 25 through 32
of 1966.
The employe resumed her registration for work in week 33 of
1966 (the week beginning August 7th and ending August 13th). In that week
she was referred by the public employment office to a retail store for a
job as a wrapper of baked goods. She reported to the store and was offered
the job at a starting rate of $1. 625 an hour for a forty-hour week. She
refused this job because she considered the rate of pay too low.
1

Applicant's refusal of the job was investigated and an initial de
terraination was issued by a deputy of the Industrial Commission holding
that applicant failed, without good cause, to accept an offer of work in week 33
of 1966 and that her eligibility for unemployment benefits was suspended start
ing with that week. This finding and decision was affirmed by a duly authorized
appeal tribunal.
The issue before the court is whether the finding that applicant became
"unemployed" in week 20* of 1966 is supported by the evidence and has a reason
able basis in law so that the canvassing period provided by sec. 108.04(8)(d)
started with week 21 of 1966,
In the instant case the facts are undisputed but permit the drawing
of more than one inference, namely, that employe became "unemployed"
or that she did not become unemployed in week 20 or week 23 of 1966. In
accordance with stated principles, the finding that employe did become "un
employed" in week 20 was an act of fact finding and is conclusive on this
court if it is supported by the record and has a reasonable basis in law.
Van Roy v. Industrial Comm. 5 Wis. (2d) 416. See also Glodowski v.
Industrial Comm. (1960) 11 Wis. (2d) 525.
Sec. 108.04(8)(a), Stats., states as follows:
"If an employe fails either to apply for work
when notified by a public employment office or to
accept work when offered to him, and such failure
was without good cause as determined by the com
mission, he shall be ineligible for the week in which
such failure occurs and thereafter until he has again
been employed within at least 4 weeks and has earned
wages equalling at least 4 times his weekly benefit rate."
Sec. 108. 04(8)(d) states:
"A claimant shall be deemed to have good cause under
par. (a) if the commission determines that his failure
related to work at a lower grade of skill or significantly
lower rate of pay than applied to him on one or more recent
jobs, and that he had not yet had a reasonable opportunity
(in view of labor market conditions and his degree of skill,
but not to exceed 6 weeks after he became unemployed)
to seek a new job substantially in line with his job skill
and prior rate of pay. " (Emphasis supplied)
*This could just as well have been week 23, the end of applicant's
vacation period and when she first registered for work at the
employment office. This facet of the case will be subsequently
developed.
2

The issue of this case turns on the meaning of the word "unemployed"
as used in sec. 108. 04(8)(d), Stats.
It is the applicant's position that unemployment does not start until
vacation and severance payments have been exhausted. Counsel for ap
plicant points out that under secs. 108.05(4)(a} and (b) and 108.05(5) such
payments are termed wages for benefit purposes. Counsel feels that the
term wages should not be restricted to employes who were actually perform
ing work. Thus, it is urged that applicant did not become unemployed until
week 34 (after exhaustion of vacation and severance pay) and therefore had
good cause in week 33 to refuse the job with lower pay, i.e., had not had a
reasonable opportunity, up to six weeks, to look for comparable employrnent.
We cannot agree with counsel's interpretation of the meaning of
"unemployed" as used in sec. 108. 04(8)(d).
Secs. 108.05(4)(a) and (b) and 108. 05(5) state that vacation pay and
severance pay shall be treated as wages "for benefit purposes." This
obviously does not mean for all purposes otherwise there would have
been no need to limit the term "wages" by the phrase "for benefit purposes."
Further, we are quite cognizant of the recent holding in Salerno v.
John Oster Mfg. Co., & Industrial Comm. of Wisconsin, 37 Wis. (2d) 433.
The facts in Salerno are easily distinguished, but the court made a statement
which we feel is apposite to the case at bar. There the question before the
court was whether an e1nploye had sufficient "weeks of employment" to qualify
for unemployment benefits. Employe argued that back pay she received
constituted wages and therefore she was employed for wages and had suf
ficient weeks of employment to qualify. The court rejected this argument
stating:
"It is undisputed that back pay received during a discharge
is the equivalent of wages for benefit purposes and that con
sequently the recipient of the back pay would be ineligible
for unemployment benefits. It does not follow, however,
that merely because back pay constitutes wages an employe
is performing wage-earning services for an employer during
the period in which he receives his back pay." (Emphasis
added)
By analogy, merely because vacation and severance pay constitute
wages for benefit purposes, it does not follow that applicant was employed
while receiving such payments within the meaning of sec. 108.04(8)(d).
In our judgment the Industrial Commission has properly inter
preted "unemployed" as used in subsection (8)(d). When your job is
eliminated (as it was here) and you have no work, you are unemployed.
That is a simple fact which cannot be gainsaid.
3

The words "unemployed", "employed", "unemployment", and
"employment" are found in numerous provisions of the Unemployment
Compensation Act and vary in meaning in accordance with the context in
which they are used. In view of the equivocal meanings to be found in the
statutes concerning these words, the meaning to be accorded the word "un
employed" as used in subsection (S)(d) must be determined from the wording
of that subsection. It should also be a meaning which will give effect to the
purpose of the subsection.
The purpose of unemployment compensation is to ease the financial
burden of losing a job. It represents an effort to tide the unemployed over
until new work can be found. Severance pay accomplishes precisely the
same purpose which accounts for the fact that one receiving severance pay
is not eligible for unemployment compensation benefits. It follows that while
an unemployed worker is receiving severance pay he should be looking for a
job in the same manner as if he were drawing unemployment compensation
benefit checks.
It can be logically argued that there is a difference between vacation
pay and severance pay. Here applicant had three weeks' vacation coming
and quite possibly she had the right to enjoy three weeks of idleness
before canvassing the market for a new job. Vacation pay is something
you earn by_V1oi-king. Severance_ pay is a bonus you receive when.discharged.
-------·--··-· .- • ·--·-.. - -· -
The record indicates applicant lost her job in week 20. Assuming
she had no duty to look for work until her earned vacation had expired,
viz, at the close of week 23, she then had a maximum of six weeks to
find comparable work. That takes us through week 29. As indicated,
the new job offer (comparable work but substantially lower pay) was '?
made in week 33 -- at least nine weeks after the vacation pay had terminated. ?
The crux of our decision is that when you are drawing "severance" pay _;)
you are "unemployed."
To accept applicant's argument would defeat the purpose of the Act.
A worker without a job would be given a paid vacation at the expense
of those contributing to the unemployment compensation fund. Applicant
argues that she has no duty to look for work until her severance pay
ends. Such reasoning results in an extension of the six weeks canvassing
period provided for by the statute. Applicant's duty to look for work
arose when she lost her job, and in no event later than the expiration of her
accumulated vacation credit. The six-week canvassing period commenced
to run by week 24, and thus she was obligated to accept the job offered her
in week 33.
Applicant had enjoyed a reasonable opportunity to seek work sub
stantially in line with her prior rate of pay. At the expiration of the six
weeks canvassing period, the law requires one to lower their sights
and accept lesser pay. The only standard applicable to wages in such
event is that they must not be substantially less favorable than those pre
vailing for similar work in the locality. This standard was clearly met by
the job offer here.
4

Applicant was not justified in refusing the offer, the decision of
the commission must be confirmed.
Counsel for the commission may prepare a judgment confirming the
findings and decision under review. A copy of the judgment should be fur
nished counsel for applicant for approval as to form.
Dated this 6th day of March, 1968.
BY THE COURT:
/s/ Richard W. Bardwell
Circuit Judge

title: LIRC Unemployment Insurance Decision — Richter
text:
STATE OF WISCONSIN CIRCUIT COURT MILWAUKEE
COUNTY
BRANCH 17
THEODORE J. RICHTER,
Plaintiff,
v. Case No: 03-CV-008710
LABOR AND INDUSTRY
REVIEW COMMISSION,
And CPP-PINKERTON'S
Defendants.
r1:
\
I
--'
Plaintiff Theodore Richter appeals the September 4, 2003, decision of the Labor
and Industry Review Commission ("the Commission"). In its decision, the Commission
found that Plaintiff voluntarily terminated his employment with his employer within the
meaning of Wis. Stat. §108.04(7)(a), that Plaintiff did not meet an exception to the
voluntary quit disqualification of the statute, and that Plaintiff therefore was not eligible
to receive unemployment insurance benefits beginning in week 49 of 2002. Plaintiff does
not dispute that he voluntarily terminated his employment. The only argument advanced
by Plaintiff is that Plaintiff was entitled to the immediate payment of benefits because he
terminated work with "good cause attributable to the employer," as provided in Wis. Stat.
§ 108.04(7)(b). This Court is not persuaded by Plaintiffs argument.
Plaintiff previously made $10.93 per hour as a security guard/lead officer at the
Bank One Plaza building for CPP-Pinkerton's, Inc. ("the employer"), which provides

security services to its clients. After the employer's contract with Bank One ended, the
employer offered Plaintiff continued employment as a patrolman at the rate of $10.00 per
hour.
Under section 108.04(7)(a), Wis. Stats., an employee who voluntarily terminates
with an employer is ineligible for benefits unless the quitting falls within a statutory
exception permitting the immediate payment of benefits. The statutory exception relied
upon by Plaintiff is Wis. Stat. §1 08.04(7)(b ), which provides that if an employee
voluntarily terminates employment with good cause attributable to the employer, he or
she is eligible for the immediate payment of unemployment benefits. "Good cause
attributable to the employer" means that the employee's resignation is caused by some
act or omission by the employer which justifies the quitting. Kessler v. Industrial
Comm., 27 Wis. 2d 398,401 (1965). It involves some fault on the employer's part and
must be "real and substantial." Id.
The Commission stated, in pertinent part:
The employee asserted that the decrease in pay and loss of supervisory
responsibilities justified his refusal of the employer's offer. The commission
finds that the decrease in pay from $10.93 to $10.00 and the lack of supervisory
duties in the new assignment, did not give the employee good cause attributable to
the employer for quitting his employment. The decrease in pay was not
substantial enough to justify the employee's decision to become unemployed
rather than continue in his work with the employer. Further, the employee was
alerted to the potential changes in the conditions of his work by the employer's
handbook.1 The employee received a copy of the handbook and it was his
1 The handbook states:
Security officer services are only contracted to the clients of Pinkerton-Burns
Securitas. You are not employed by the facility to which you are assigned.
Based on this condition of employment you can expect transfers among various
clients, a varied work schedule/work week and different rates of pay and related
benefits as dictated by the client contract. Pinkerton-Burns-Securitas encourages
you to use the appropriate chain of command with questions regarding working
hours, rates of pay, benefits or similar subjects.
Record at 2.

responsibility to read the handbook. The conditions of the work offered were not
substantially less favorable to the employee than existed for similar work in his
labor market.
(Record at 3).
In his brief, Plaintiff argues that the offered position involved (1) a substantial
drop in skill level and (2) a 13.08% decrease in final rate of pay (after health insurance
premiums are considered). According to Plaintiff, the position at the Bank One building
encompassed supervisory duties and technical job skills that involve building knowledge, •
computer literacy and emergency response procedures. Plaintiff argues that the employer
is at fault for losing the Bank One contract. Plaintiff also argues that the Commission did
not consider the insurance contribution in recognizing the real wage loss, and did not
address the technical job skills that were required for each position. According to
Plaintiff, when these issues are considered, the employer's failure to offer a similar
position in terms of pay rate and job skill is "real and substantial."
Although the employer testified at the hearing that Plaintiff would be responsible
for 25% of the health insurance premium, the record does not indicate the dollar amount
that Plaintiff would be required to pay. This Court will not consider evidence that has not
been offered to the Commission. See Weibel v. Clark, 87 Wis. 2d 696, 708 (1979).
Plaintiff also testified that one of the reasons for declining the employer's offer
was because it involved a significant drop in skill level. (Hearing Transcript at 19, 21).
This Court has no reason to conclude that the Commission did not consider this portion
of the record.
The Commission's determination that Plaintiff had not demonstrated "good
cause" for terminating her employment within the meaning of section 108.04(7)(b) is

entitled to great weight deference. Klatt v. Labor & Indus. Review Comm 'n, 266 Wis. 2d
1038, 1049 (Ct. App. 2003). Therefore, this court will not substitute its view of the law
for that of the Conunission and will su;tain the Commission's conclusion oflaw ifit is
reasonable. Brown v. Labor & Indus, Review Comm'n, 267 Wis. 2d 31, 46 (2003). The
Commission's conclusion of law will be sustained even if an alternative view of the law
is just as reasonable or even more reasonable. Id. at 46-47. In this case, the Conunission
could reasonably find that the wage reduction, drop in skill level, and loss of supervisory
duties were not substantial enough to justify Plaintiffs decision to terminate his
employment. After all, the unemployment compensation statute was not intended to
provide relief when reasonable work is available which the employee can but will not do.
Roberts v. Industrial Commission, 2 Wis. 2d 399, 403 (1957).
ORDER
THEREFORE, based upon a thorough review of the record, it is hereby ordered
that the September 4, 2003, decision of the Commission is AFFIRMED.
Dated at Milwaukee, Wisconsin, this "3il1day of June, 2004.

Francis Wasielewski
Circuit Court Judge

STATE OF WISCONSIN CffiCUIT COURT JUNEAU COUNTY

BACKGROUND
The matter before the court is a review of a ~ecision of the Labor and Industry Review
Comrniss1on (hereinafter "LIRC11). The relevant facts as found by the LIRC are as follows:
All plaintiffs were federal funded employees. of the Department of Military Affairs, the Adjutant
General (hereinafter employer) with federally controlled funding. The employer received notice
from the National Guard Bureau that there would be a shortage of federal funding commencing
in the 1995 fiscal year. The National Guard Bureau authorized funds for voluntary early
. . . .
'
retirement authority and voluntary separation incentive pay to federally funded employees that
met certain criteria. The employer notified qualified employees offering the voluntary early
buyouts or voluntary separation incentive pay, or both. The plaintiffs in this case met the
criteria involved and voluntarily chose to accept the employers' offer for early retirement or a
buyout package, or both, and terminated their employment. The voluntary terminations occurred
during the period between December 31, 1994, and February 4, 1995. Thereafter plaintiffs filed
for employment benefits and during the months of February and March, 1995, the Department

of Labor and Industry Human Relations (hereinafter "DILHR") determined that each plaintiff
had terminated employment in lieu of termination of another employee within the meaning of
Section 108.04(7)(am) of the Wisconsin Statutes. The employer appealed such initial
determinations and after a hearing before the administrative Jaw judge on June 5, 1995, an
appealed tribunal decision was issued on June 12, 1995, affirming the initial DILHR •
determinations. That decision was appealed to the LIRC and on November 9, 1995, and in an
amended decision of November 15, 1995, the LIRC issued a decision and memorandum opinion
reversing the appeal tribunal. The LIRC found that plaintiffs terminated their employment
within the meaning of Section 108.04(7)(a), Stats., and that plaintiffs "quitting was not for any
reason constituting an exception to that section." Plaintiffs filed a summons and complaint
appealing the commission's decision.
The issue before this court is whether or not the LIRC erred in concluding that each of
the plaintiffs failed to demonstrate that his or her work with the employer was suspended or
terminated in lieu of suspension or termination by the employer of any other employee's work,
within the meaning of Section 108.4(7)(a), Stats.; and whether plaintiffs' eligibility for
unemployment compensation benefits was suspended for voluntarily terminating their
employment with employer within the meaning of Section 108.04(7)(a), Stats. Thus the issue
is whether the plaintiffs resigned voluntarily rendering themselves ineligible for unemployment
compensation or whether plaintiffs' resignations fell within one of the exceptions to the
ineligibility for voluntary termination rules.
Relevant statutes include the following:
Section 102.23(1) JUDICIAL REVIEW
2

(a) The findings of fact made by the commission acting within its
powers shall, in the absence of fraud, be conclusive. The order or
award granting if denying compensation, either interlocutory of
final, whether judgment has been rendered on it or not, is subject
to review only as provided in this section and not under ch. 227 or
s. 801.02. Within 30 days after the date of an order or award
made by the commission either originally or after the filing of a
petition for review with the department under s. 102.18 any party
aggrieved thereby may by serving a complaint as provided in par.
(b) and filing the summons and complaint with the clerk of the
circuit court commence, in circuit court, an action against the
commission for the review of the order or award, in which action
the adverse party shall also be made a defendant. If the circuit
court is satisfied that a party in interest has been prejudiced
because of an exceptional delay in the receipt of a copy of any
finding or order, it may extend the time in which an action may be
commenced by an additional 30 days. The proceedings shall be in
the circuit court of the county where the plaintiff resides, except
that if the plaintiff is a state agency, the proceedings si)all be in the
circuit court of the county where the defendant resides. The
proceedings may be brought in any circuit court if all parties
stipulate and that court agrees.
(e) Upon such hearing, the court may confirm or set aside such
order or award; and any judgment which may theretofore have
been rendered thereon; but the same shall be set aside only upon
the following grounds:
1. That the commission acted without or in excess of its
powers.
2. That the order or award was procured by fraud.
3. · That the findings of fact by the commission do not support
the order or award.
Section 102.23(6) JUDICIAL REVIEW
If the commission's order or award depends on any fact found by
the commission, the court shall not substitute its judgment for that
of the commission as to the weight or credibility of the evidence
on any finding of fact. The court may, however, set aside the
commission's order or award and remand the case to the
commission if the commission's order or award depends on any
material and controverted finding of fact that is not support by
credible and substantial evidence.
3

Section 108.04(7) VOLUNTARY TERMINATION OF
EMPLOYMENT
(a) If any employee terminates work with an employing unit, the
employee is ineligible to receive benefits until 4 weeks have
elapsed since the end of the week in which the termination occurs
and the employee earns wages after the week in which the
termination occurs equal to at least 4 times the employee's weekly
benefit rate under s. 108.05(1) in employment or other work
covered by the unemployment compensation law of any state of the
federal government. ..
(am) Paragraph (a) does not apply if the department determines
that the suspension or termination of the claimant's work was in
lieu of a suspension or termination by the employer of another
employee's work. The claimant shall not be deemed unavailable
for the claimant's work with the employer by reason of such
suspension or termination.
Section 108.09(7) JUDICIAL REVIEW
(a) The depart_ment or, either party may commence action for the
judicial review of a decision of the commission under this chapter
after exhausting the remedies provided under this section if the
party or the department has commenced such action in accordance
with s. 102.23 within 30 days after a decision of the commission
is mailed to a party's last-known address.
(b) Any judicial review under this chapter shall be confined to
questions of law, and the provisions of ch. 102 with respect to
judicial review of orders and awards shall likewise apply to any
decision of the commission reviewed under this section ...
As provided in sec. 102.23(l)(a), Stats., the findings of fact made by the commission in the
absence of fraud are conclusive on this court. Section 102.23(1)(a), Stats., provides that the
court may confirm or set aside a commission decision but if the commission acted without or
in excess of its powers; that the order or award was procured by fraud; or that the findings of
fact by the commission do not support the order or award. Section 102.23(6), Stats., provides
that the court is not to substitute its judgment for that of the commission as to the weight or
4

credibility of the evidence on a finding of fact. Furthermore, the commission's findings of fact
must be upheld if they are supported by credible and substantial evidence, Princess House Inc.
· v. DILHR, 111 Wis. 2d 46, 54, 330 N.W.2d 169 (1983); Nottleson v. ILHR Dept., 94 Wis.
2d 106, 114, 287 N.W.2d 763 (1980). It is not within the purview of the reviewing court to
weigh the evidence presented, Farmers Mill of Athens. Inc. v. ILHR Dept.. 97 Wis. 2d 576,
579-80, 294 N.W.'.i.d 39 (Ct. App. 1980); Vandezande v. ILHR Dept., 70 Wis.2d 1086, 1097,
236 N.W.2d 255 (1975). The inferences drawn by the commission are considered acts of fact
finding and the inference derived by it is conclusive. Wehr Steel Co. v. ILHR Dept.. 106 Wis.
2d 111, 118, 315 N.W.2d 357 (1982); Universal Foundry v. ILHR Dept., 86 Wis. 2d 582, 589,
273 N.W. 2d 324 (1979). The reviewing court is not to ascertain whether additional findings
should have been made or could have been sustained by the evidence. Appleton Electric Co.
v. Minor. 91 Wis. 2d 825, 829, 284 N.W.2d 99 (1979).
The judicial standard of review of an agency's application of a statute which is
administered is to apply the "great weight" standard to the agency's decision. Sauk County v.
WERC. 165 Wis. 2d 406, 413, 477 N.W. 2d 267 (1991); DILHR v. LIRC. 161 Wis. 2d 231,
243, 467 N. W.2d 545 (1991); State of Wisconsin v. LIRC. 113 Wis. 2d 107, 109, 334 N. W.
2d 279 (1983).
The reviewing court may not substitute its judgment for the administrative agency's
application of a statute to the specific facts where reasonable basis exists in law for the agency's
interpretation. Klusendorf Chevrolet-Buick. Inc. v. LIRC. 110 Wis. 2d 328, 331-332, 328
N.W.2d 890 (Ct. App. 1982); Pabst v. Department of Taxation. 19 Wis. 2d 313, 323-24, 120
N. W.2d 77 (1963).
5

Furthermore, if the commission's conclusion is reasonable, the reviewing court shall
sustain that conclusion even though an alternative view may be equally as reasonable. United
Way of Greater Milwaukee. Inc. v. DILHR. 105 Wis. 2d 447, 453, 313 N.W.2d 85 (Ct. App,
1981); Farmers Mill of Athens. Inc. v. ILHR Dept.. 97 Wis. 2d 576, 580 294 N.W.2d 39 (Ct.
App.1980). The reviewing court should not disturb the commission's judgment concerning a
question of law if there exists a rational basis for the commission's conclusion. Dairy
Equipment Company v. ILHR Dept.,95 Wis. 2d 319, 327, 290 N.W.2d 330 (1980); Milwaukee
County v. ILHR Dept.. 80 Wis. 2d 445, 446, 259 N.W.2d (1977).
DECISION
Section 108.04(7)(a); Stats., provides that an employee is ineligible for unemployment
compensation benefits if the employee voluntarily terminates his or her employment with the
employer; unless the quitting falls within a statutory exemption permitting immediate
unemployment compensation benefit payment. Plaintiffs' argument is that the statutory
exemption provided under Section 108.04(7)(am), Stats., allo'!Vs them to collect unemployment
compensation benefits because they voluntarily chose early retirement or buyouts and terminated
their employment to save the jobs of other employees.
The evidence in the record does not establish that plaintiffs' termination of employment
was in lieu of the suspension or termination ofanother employee's work The plaintiffs' quitting
did not involve a direct tradeoff off their employment in lieu of the suspension or termination
of another identified employee. The record establishes that the employer did not specifically
target any employee for termination or suspension and, in fact, no employee was ever suspended
or terminated. Plaintiffs would have continued in their employment had they not accepted the
6

employer's offer of a voluntary early retirement or buyout or both, which included a significant
financial benefit to them. Plaintiffs' decision to terminate their employment was a voluntary
action which amounts to quitting.
The record indicates the employer engaged in a reduction of force exercise which was
required by the National Guard Bureau to economically justify buyouts and early retirements to
individuals meeting specific criteria. The record shows that the employer was not required to
implement a reduction of force or to suspend or terminate any employee. The employer
successfully used alternatives to avoid the necessity for involuntary termination or suspension
of any employees. Furthermore, there is no evidence in the record that even if the employer
had been forced to suspend or terminate employees due to budgetary constraints, that any of the
plaintiffs had been targeted for suspension or termination in lieu of other employees.
Section 108.04(7)(am), Stats., sets forth a specific exception to the general quitting
disqualification and provides:
Paragraph (a) does not apply if the department determines that the
suspension or termination of the claimant's work was in lieu of a _
suspension or termination by the employer of another employee's
work. The claimant shall not be deemed unavailable for claimant's
work with the employer by reason of such suspension or
termination.
That statutory exception can be rationally and reasonably interpreted to require a direct
correlation between the employment of the individual claiming benefits and a person identified
for suspension or termination. The LIRC found credible and reasonable evidence that the
plaintiffs had an option to continue employment with the employer but chose instead to accept
the offer of voluntary buyout or retirement. Plaintiffs fail to establish that another employee had
been identified for suspension or termination at any point if they continued employment with the
7

' '
employer. Thus, there was a rational and reasonable basis for the commission's decision.
Since the commission's interpretation of the statute is reasonable, rational and consistent
with the legislative intent, it will not be disturbed by t.his court. Therefore, the decision of the
J
-S
commission is confirmed in all respects..

This is an action to review decisions of the Labor and
Industry Re-view Commission respecting unemployment compensation
benefits of the Plaintiff, Timothy J. Weiss. The sole issue
raised by the Plaintiff is that the procedure followed before the
administrative law judge violated his rights to·due process.
The· scope of judicial review in this matter is set forth in
Section 102.23(1) Wis. Stats~ The bases ~or setting aside a
commission determination are limited t.o the·. following: .
"1. That the commission acted without or in eXC$SS of
its powers.
2. That the order or award was procured by fraud.
3 . That the findings of fact by the co:rhnd: s s i_on do not
support the order or award."
The scope of judicial review has been addressed in a
multitude of cases. It is sufficient for the purposes of this
case to note that no issue of fraud is raised nor is there any
issue respecting the sufficiency of the evidence to sup~ort the
findings of the Commission. ·The sole issue is whether there was
a due process violation sufficient 'to warrant relief to the
1

Plaintiff.
A brief was filed by the Plaintiff, a response brief was
filed by the commission, and a reply brief was filed by the
Plaintiff. I have reviewed the hearing record, eacJ:i: of the
briefs filed by the parties, and the -cases cited in each brief.
It should first be noted that the Plaintiff does not argue
that there is any question regarding the honesty or integrity of
the administrative law judge. Although Plaintiff's initial brief
implies some bias on the part of the administrative law judge,

this case. In each of the cases cited by the Plaintiff, there

The concern expressed by the Plaintiff is not without some
substance. However, the administrative law judge is charged with
the responsibility of developing a record. That is of particular

My review of this record leads to the conclusion that there
was no violation of the Plaintiff's rights to due process. The
Plaintiff disavows any allegation of·bias and acknowledges the
presumption of honesty and integrity on the part of adjudicators
in administrative proceedings, State ex rel, DeLuca v. common
council, 72 Wis.2d 672 (1976). To the extent that there is an
implication of bias in Plaintiff's original argument, I find that
none is shown in the record. Furthermore, the rulings made by
the administrative ·1a.;r judge respecting the a.dmission of exhibits
into the record did not result in a denial of due process.
Situations in which one party is not represented by counsel
creates some difficulty for a hearing examiner, similar to the
difficulty that can occur when prose litigants appear before
courts. It would be best if all parties were represented by
counsel who thoroughly develop a record in matters of this type.
